subtopic: OIL SUBSTITUTION AND CONSERVATION ACT CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the amendment to Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Elome Insulation Program Act, because I think this is one of the few programs that has been used to help thousands of Canadians who showed an earnest desire to change their living habits.
Under the Canadian Oil Substitution Program introduced in 1980 by a Liberal Government, taxable grants of up to $800 were available as partial payment for the cost of converting from oil to heating systems operating on natural gas, electric power, propane, wood or other forms of renewable energy. According to the present legislation, the program expires on December 31, 1990. The proposed Bill provides that the deadline will be moved up to March 31 of this year, which is in about a week. We believe that by asking to have the bill withdrawn and referred to the appropriate parliamentary committee, we can make the transition period easier for Canadian consumers.
1 must emphasize that Bill C-24 represents a threat for direct action programs. These programs are designed for consumers. They also directly concern families and homeowners. Thus, by their very nature, they have a very special character. Eliminating these programs means that we are going to deprive Canadian families of funds earmarked for them by the Federal Government.
It is important to realize the impact these cuts will have. The Canadian Home Insulation Program is designed for homeowners who want to conserve energy. They can obtain up to $500 to help pay for costs incurred.
As for the Canadian Oil Substitution Program, homeowners have taken advantage of this program to convert from oil to another kind of heating system. The $800 grant was very well received and has been an incentive for Canadians to do the requisite conversion.
The benefits of both programs now extend well beyond the dollar value of the grants. These programs are meant for consumers who are worried about the price of oil for home heating. The people who wanted to take advantage of the programs were counting on an expiry date on December 31, 1990, according to the information given by the federal Government. The problem is, however, that many Canadians who felt that a program set up by the Liberal Government would be maintained by the new Progressive Conservative Government, are now seeing another series of cuts, which of course, translate as lay-offs in the construction industry.
The Government claims that everything will be all right, and that people will still convert their heating system. The Government claims that Canadians are well aware of the options they have as far as energy is concerned. Many are. And they can afford to be because they have been able to take advantage of these programs. However, there are Canadians who will not be able to take advantage of these programs because they were waiting for the weather to get better before starting work on these projects.
The Government must revise its position and postpone consideration of the Bill if it wants to maintain its credibility before the Canadian public. This would give people a chance to have their systems installed, and it would also be more convenient for installers and suppliers of natural gas and heating equipment to install the systems at a time of the year when conditions are more favourable.
The Government, by ignoring requests for extending the program, gives the impression it does not care about the average Canadian. I think Canadians are going to find it very hard to accept the fact that these programs have been scuttled. I do not think the Government has given the needs of the average Canadian enough thought. I do not think the Government opposite realizes that Canadians had great confidence in this program and not just because of the grants. And once again, the people who are going to suffer will be Canadians on set or low incomes and the unemployed.
As Members of the Liberal Party of Canada, we ask this Government to have the courage to accept the amendment we are proposing today, which will allow Canadians who want to take advantage of the program to do so. The program should be maintained so that people will not have to suffer the inconvenience of installing equipment in the winter.
The Government maintains that Canadians will be able to save energy without these programs as well. However, it will soon realize that removing the programs will create a number of problems. It is too bad that the Government insists on making cuts that will affect those Canadians who are most in need.
Why should the Canadian consumer always be made to bear the brunt of such cuts, especially when a number of Ministers have run up interior decorating bills for their offices that are entirely unreasonable.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Government should inflict these program cuts on Canadians without giving them prior notice, and I fail to see what the Progressive Conservative Government has to lose by taking a conciliatory stance with the people who elected them on September 4 last year.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this legislation a second

time. I am interested in debating it again because I feel it is important legislation and, if we can make our position sufficiently clear, the Government might reconsider the legislation. It is somewhat discouraging that a motion to terminate debate was moved this morning to bring the legislation to an immediate vote. That indicates that the Government is not listening to what is being said on this side of the House.
It is important for the Government to listen to the arguments of Opposition Members, because we represent our constituents and the views of Canadians. The Government promised to be sensitive to public opinion and the needs of people. The Government could demonstrate its capacity to be sensitive by listening and responding to this debate. But rather than doing that, it has chosen once again to limit debate. It is sad. The Conservative Party for many years has indicated its commitment to parliamentary democracy. One would think that a Party which is committed to parliamentary democracy would be interested in having open debate in this Chamber and using that debate to improve legislation rather than viewing debate as an obstacle to the objectives which it has unilaterally set. But, rather than having respect for the House of Commons and for serious debate, we are getting arrogance and an unbending attitude toward decisions which the Government has already taken, instead of thoughtful reconsideration of the positions which it has already established.
The Government may be encouraging inadvertently the kind of action which the Senate recently took with its second sober thought on legislation which the House had passed. I would not want to see that repeated. I am afraid that if the Government, by virtue of its deafness in regard to reasonable argument, proceeds with this legislation and does not listen to reason, we might be giving more ammunition to members in the other place. They could say that the House of Commons is not really doing its job, that the House has not considered all of the aspects of this legislation, and that they will be forced to take a second sober look at it. That would not be good for Parliament. It is not good government, and it is not good for the people of Canada.
The legislation which is before us today limits the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program. Both of those programs are valuable and have demonstrated their effectiveness. With COSP, targets were set for the conversion of heating systems in homes from oil to gas, solar or electricity. Those targets were being met. COSP uses the public dollar to encourage conservation and change in home heating systems. That program was working. One has to wonder why the Government chose to eliminate a program which was achieving its objectives. Those objectives were legitimate and served a worth-while public purpose.
Why would the Government cut that program and at the same time substantially increase funding for the Prime Minister's Office? Why does the Government want to spend more on bureaucrats in the PMO than on a program which is serving a worth-while public need? This program helped people to meet the ever-rising cost of heating their homes.
Oil Substitution Act
This is a Government, Mr. Speaker, which is moving to deregulate oil pricing in this country. It is seeking to take the ceiling off any future rises in oil costs, which means that Canadians will be subject to the whims of the international market when it comes to the cost of heating their own homes. It is not simply being subject to a free market which responds to the pressures of competition; it is being the victim of a market which is dominated by large mutinational corporations, by a cartel. It is hard to understand why this Government is moving, on the one hand, to remove regulations which seek to protect Canadians from the vagaries of the international oil prices and exposing us to the whims of international measures and, on the other hand, is removing the program which would help us to adjust to increasing oil prices. These are government actions which put the ordinary Canadian in a vice which squeezes him from both sides. This is a Government which allows oil prices to rise at the same time that it takes away the incentives for moving away from reliance upon oil.
When this Government was running for office, it projected an image as a humanitarian party, a party which was concerned about Canadians and which was going to help people. I would challenge Hon. Members on the Government side to rise and explain to Hon. Members on this side how cutting off these conservation programs helps ordinary Canadians. How does removing financial assistance to convert from oil to gas, solar or electricity help people? In what way does that make sense? The move on the part of the Government to cut the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program is part of an over-all strategy to cut public spending and, by cutting public spending, we will reduce the deficit and somehow, magically, the economy will be revived and everyone will be affluent. There are good reasons to question the cost-cutting strategy of the Government. I see I have one minute, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, several years ago a very important, very famous article was written by a British scientist named Amory Lovins. He put forward a very striking thesis, which was that industrial

March 21, 1985
Oil Substitution Act
nations really have two choices in the development of energy resources. First there is the conventional way called the "hard path", which is the big megaprojects, the large-scale industrial energy projects and the massive capital expenditures into huge developments. He countered that by saying a far more effective use would be what is called the "soft path", which is to begin developing energy conservation techniques which could be localized, decentralized, could be applied with a flexibility to the local community and could be used to create jobs, major savings and to conserve against the undue reduction of our renewable resources.
That was a message and a thought which was well taken at the time. In this country, to our credit, we began some of the most extensive developments of alternate energy programs of any industrialized country in the world. We invested in the National Research Council. We established a new Crown Corporation, Canertech. We invested a lot of money in programs like the Canadian Home Insulation Program and the conversion program.
We recognized that we should not put all of our eggs into one basket, that we should not only try to substantially increase the conventional oil and gas reserves but we should also provide for a much broader, more flexible and diverse system for continuing Canada's self-sufficiency in the energy area. That approach proved to be accurate, Mr. Speaker, and from 1977 through to 1984 we found that across Canada in places like Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, the northern interior of British Columbia and western Canada, with respect to programs which are under debate today, small communities began developing their own individualized energy sources. New firms were started, small businesses emerged to provide for the application of these programs. People went to work.
Not only did these things happen in a conventional manner, but all kinds of innovative ways of converting energy were developed. We really started a new industry in this country. There was an opportunity for new entrepreneurship to emerge, not only in the big cities but in many small towns and communities in more remote regions.
This project was not just energy conservation. It also became the stimulus for the development of a new category of small businesses in Canada. In my own Province of Manitoba, for example, over 100,000 residential units were able to make use of these programs. Several hundred new businesses were started. People were trained in this area. But now the Government, again praying at the sacred font of its so-called cut-back philosophy, is going to wipe that out. It is going to do away with it.
There is no reason or rationale for that. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) do not give any reason for doing away with these programs. They just say that everyone has to share the pain equally. We all have to pay for the reduction in the deficit. But why cut this program? Why not cut some other area where we don't have small businesses being created, we don't have the very clear opportunity to provide for alternate energy production, we don't have development of new entrepreneurs across Canada in the small business area and where we don't have, in particular, the remote regions and the small towns being the major beneficiaries?
This is something we see time and time again, Mr. Speaker. This is a Government which is not interested in the average citizen of this country. It is not interested in the small community or in small businesses. Nor is the Government interested, really, in thinking in any kind of innovative way. I don't know who the Government listens to these days. We are told it is consulting but I think it is starting to chase its own tail. I think it is simply drinking its own bath water. Government is not listening to Canadians; if it was, it would not be doing away with this program. It would not be doing away with a program which saves our very precious energy resources.
Canada is using up its energy sources faster than any other country in the world. We have what you would call a mature energy-producing area in western Canada, but not many new fields are being discovered. We have exploratory fields in Hibernia and the Beaufort, but that is expensive energy and hard to get. So why would we be cutting back on programs which eliminate reliance on hard to get and expensive energy resources? Why would we be penalizing the Canadian consumer over the next few decades.
The only reason, and we keep coming back to it, is this curious, almost religious doctrinaire approach of cutting back government expenditures because the Government says that will be the cause of something miraculous. Yet we see this same Government spending $60 million or $70 million on new military uniforms. How can we justify that additional cost when it is compared with the possibility of developing alternate energy sources? One finds it hard to explain because there is no rationale. I am sure that the members of our Defence forces could have gotten along for a few more years with the same uniforms if it meant that Canadian consumers could have converted to a less expensive fuel and continued to reinsulate their homes and commercial buildings. It really defies logical and rational explanation.
This attitude is reflected in other areas as well, Mr. Speaker. What is perhaps most tragic is that the Government, through its cuts in funding for the NRC and other research organizations, has in one fell swoop destroyed Canada's leadership in developing alternate energy. This leadership would have provided us with the potential for new exports as well as the potential for developing new knowledge-intensive industries which would be unique in our country. The Government has taken us from a position of leadership in that field to the position of being a backwater.
It is hard to treat seriously in any way the comments of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) or the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), or other Members of the front benches who say they want Canada to be competitive. They say we will increase sales and have economic renewal at the same time that the very basis and foundation for development in those areas has been wiped

away. We had already established that leadership. Other countries came to Canada to look at the progress we were making, but now this Government has wiped that leadership out. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate because the programs which are being axed by the Government have been of tremendous importance and have helped thousands of home owners in Winnipeg improve their homes and use less energy. Furthermore, these programs have provided hundreds of jobs for people who otherwise would have been unemployed.
I am glad that the Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) is here because he can confirm the fact that in my constituency, the constituency of the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) and the constituency of St. Boniface there are many homes that were built between 50 and 75 years ago that are very energy inefficient. fuel, whether it is gas, oil or electricity, due to the insufficient amount of insulation that was installed in those homes.
Despite the proven record of these successful programs, the Government is proposing their elimination. In recent years we have seen the cost of energy double and quadruple. This has had a drastic effect on jobs and the lifestyle of ordinary citizens. When these programs encourage energy conservation, surely any sensible government would encourage and even promote such programs.
The provisions of the Canadian Oil Substitution Program made financial assistance available in order to convert heating systems from oil to a non-oil-fired system. Since we are rapidly coming to the end of the supply of relatively cheap oil that was discovered before 1970, we will have to import oil, begin to produce oil which will be found off the Atlantic coast, in the Arctic or which will be produced by the tar sands. Surely every member of the Conservative Party must realize that when we have to start using that oil we are going to increase greatly the cost of heating our homes, as well as increase the cost of energy use in our plants and factories. Every Member of Parliament should be interested in promoting conservation.
These programs have been very successful. Why has the Government brought in legislation to end these programs? We have not had a single sensible explanation. The only explanation is that the Government wants to save money in the short run. What we will get is short-term gain for long-term pain.
It has been estimated that under these programs we should effect two million conversions of heating systems by 1990. This would mean a tremendous reduction in the use of oil for heating, especially in many of the older homes in our cities and rural areas. They are usually inhabited by people in the low and middle-income levels, people who can least afford the increased cost of heating which they have experienced in recent years and which they will experience again in the next few years, particularly if they cannot convert from oil to gas.
Almost one million units have already been converted. The program is only half completed yet the Government proposes to axe it. As a result of the program that was implemented, we have been saving over 50 million barrels of oil a year. That is oil which cannot be replaced except at tremendous cost to the country and to our people. New oil, which we will probably bring on stream from the tar sands, the Atlantic and the Arctic, will cost the Canadian consumer and Canadian industry users very much more than what it has cost up to now. It has been estimated that each home converted from oil saves the home owner or the renter about $600 a year in heating costs. Why stop a program which has been so successful?
It is interesting to look at the debate and how the Parties reacted to the proposal when the Bill was brought forward in 1981. There was virtually no debate. It lasted not much more than an hour or two and it received the unanimous support of all Parties.
Let me quote a few sentences from a speech made, I presume, on behalf of the then Official Opposition, the
March 21, 1985

Progressive Conservative Party, by the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), a former Cabinet Minister in the Diefenbaker Government and one of the longest serving Members in this House. I quote from a speech the Hon. It is a good philosophy to get as many people in the low technology systems as possible to move away from the consumption of oil. It is particularly good if the alternative is cheaper not only than the present price of oil but the future price as well.
I could not have put it any better than the Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. It should be obvious to all Canadians that the program which this Government is now proposing to end was and is a common-sense program under which no one can lose, neither consumers nor governments. The only ones to gain are the oil companies which will be able to make bigger profits with much more expensive oil for which we will be paying in the very near future.
I see I have very little time left, but let me deal with one other aspect of the adverse effects that we will get when this program is ended. In converting, jobs were provided for hundreds and thousands of people who are not highly skilled, not expensively trained, people in the main who are unemployed. In converting homes and in insulating homes, hundreds of thousands of people in my city, in other cities and in many rural areas were able to find work and were employed rather than unemployed and drawing unemployment insurance. This program, when it is terminated, will end the jobs of at least hundreds and thousands of people who have been able to find work as a result of these programs.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to speak against this closure motion, this time allocation
motion. The motion intends, by whatever means, to cut off debate. It is quite unnecessary. The Government should be listening not just to the words but to the points which have been made on this side of the House. It should be showing a willingness to reconsider the mistake it made in introducing this Bill. The Government shows no interest in considering the points which have been made. It simply wants to use its majority to hammer this matter through within the time limits imposed in this motion.
Basically this is part of the mistake which the Government has been following for six months, the mistake of cutting back on money available to the large majority of Canadians with ordinary incomes, including those on low incomes, while increasing directly and indirectly the money available to large corporations, such as the oil companies in this case, and to large investors.
This is simply one element of the program followed by the Government which it claims will bring recovery. So far it has completely failed to show any serious result for ordinary Canadians. Unemployment is where it was, and there is no prospect of any serious improvement. The Government is failing to provide the basic necessary market for goods and services which Canadians could produce if economic institutions permitted them to do so.
With this Bill, the Government is cutting back money available for switching from oil to other forms of heating and cutting back the amount of money available for insulation, which would save oil. It is not proposing to cut back the money for exploration to discover new oil. It is proposing to cut back, through this legislation, the money that would be saved and the oil that would be saved by conservation. While they call themselves Conservatives, they are acting against the principle of conservation.
Many people in my riding have used this program and many more would like to use it. Both the off oil and CHIP programs have had good success so far. Many people have seen the value of them. They have seen what their neighbours have saved and they are interested in taking them up.
Not all these people could do that right away. There are some very low-income home owners in my riding who cannot always take advantage of a program instantly. This winter, with shortages of equipment, it has not been possible for everyone to take advantage. It is a great mistake for this Government to cut off this program. It is a mistake from the point of view of the majority of ordinary Canadians. It may not be a mistake from the point of view of the oil companies, but they do not act in the interest of this country. When the wealthiest sector of industry in this country, except for the banks, asks for bigger and bigger hand-outs, it is not serving the interest of this country. Instead, it is trying to hold this country to ransom.
When in opposition, Members opposite claimed to support the fact that a barrel of oil saved by the actions of small business people, those who do the conversion of the furnaces

March 21, 1985

and the insulation of the homes, is worth more than a barrel of oil to be found in the Beaufort Sea. It costs less to save a barrel of oil through conservation than it costs to take it out of the Beaufort Sea or out of the tar sands. Furthermore, it provides jobs where they are needed. Very few of Canada's two million unemployed are in the Beaufort or even in northern Alberta. The vast majority are in Canadian cities. That is where the conservation work is to be done, in the cities of Canada. That is where the jobs should be created. That is where there are hundreds of thousands of people willing and able to do this conservation work and save the oil reserves of this country.
It seems that this Government is afraid that there might be some oil left in the ground when it leaves office in a few years. It wants to dig it all, or as much as possible, out now. Some of us think a little farther ahead. Quite apart from who will be the Government, some of us have children and grandchildren. Others expect to have children and grandchildren.
I see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) smiling. He agrees with me. I do not know the details, but I am sure he is looking forward to an increase in his descendants. It would be good if we could have some oil for his descendants, for mine, for those of all others here and those whom we represent.
We do not have to be in such a mad rush to take all the oil and burn it. There are excellent conservation programs which, as I say, cost less than digging the oil. It would leave some of the oil in the ground. Perhaps in future it could be developed more cheaply. If it is not needed, let us leave it there. Let us not squander the oil. Then it would be too late to pay people to conserve it.
It has been argued that the Government should not be intervening in this way, that it should let the private home owners do it. For some private home owners, that is all right, they can pay. However, for many it is a borderline question. Without this assistance, they are not likely to do it.
There have been other cuts in the incomes of home owners. The $500 total of tax and other imposts was laid on the people this fall by this Government. That reduced the money available for a project like this. There have been wage cuts; that is, cuts compared to cost of living. A number of people have become unemployed since that time, especially poor home owners. It is those people who should have the continued benefit of this program of changing from oil to other forms of energy and insulating their houses in order to save oil.
What we are asking is simply that the Government withdraw the Bill or make some serious proposal for amendments to it before it leaves this House. We would like some assurance that the Government has listened, not only to the speakers on this side of the House, but to the letters that have come in from both home owners and small business people who believe that this is a good program. It is not only in the interest of the small businesses, their workers and the home owners, but in the interest of all the people of Canada to save that oil. It is also in the interest of all the people of Canada to save the oil
Oil Substitution Act
used in eastern Canada which has to be imported at a higher cost.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his colleagues weep daily over the deficit. They use the deficit as an excuse for all kinds of things they do which hurt the people of Canada, such as the budget cuts last fall. Here is a way to reduce the deficit without hurting the people of Canada. The Government can reduce the amount of money that has to be spent on offshore oil, but it does not want to do that.
Clearly anything that reduces the money that goes to the oil companies is not what the Prime Minister and his colleagues want. They want to fatten the oil companies and perhaps the banks as well. They do not care what it costs the people of Canada. They do not care whether we squander our oil so that our children and grandchildren will not have any. The motion to terminate the debate was a great mistake, but not a surprising one. It is completely in line with what this Government has been doing by way of spreading paper around the country, pretending consultation. Oil Substitution Act
If anyone were to take the time to look at the debates regarding Bill C-24, they would notice that almost without exception there has been nothing but praise for these two federal Government programs. Members have indicated how successful the programs have been. The oil substitution program has displaced some 32,000 barrels of oil or more. The home insulation program has also been successful in saving over 28,000 barrels of oil. The grand total of the two is a saving of about 60,000 barrels of oil per day.
Not only have these two programs saved a tremendous amount of oil but people for the first time have taken seriously the possibility of using alternate energy sources. We are finally moving out of the preaching stage when it comes to using alternate energy. These two programs have encouraged people to actually do it.
In the constituency which I represent there are a tremendous amount of wood products available, and people have converted from oil to woodburning furnaces. They have taken a local energy source that would otherwise be wasted and utilized it to save money. That is why this program has been very important to the average working family in Canada. It has been important to people who do not have high incomes and who are living in a region like northern Ontario where the winters are long and cold. Saving money on home heating is a very big issue there. It has been people with average incomes who have used the home insulation program and have conserved energy in their own homes. In addition to that, they have gone off oil, an expensive form of energy, to something like wood. Other people have been experimental and are using solar energy. In some places they have even been utilizing wind energy. However, the most important conversion program has been that of oil to natural gas.
The federal Government has had a program allowing natural gas companies to extend their systems with the use of a federal Government subsidy. That program is not being discontinued. The natural gas network system is still being expanded. In the area I represent, that program will be reactivated again this spring or early summer as soon as the frost is out of the ground. However, my constituents have said to me: "We cannot take advantage of that program any longer. The gas network system is being expanded but we are out in the cold just because we did not apply before last November. How did we know? We inquired of you about the program and you said that we could take advantage of it when we were able to afford it because we had until 1990". Now, following the election, these people have discovered that it is not 1990, it is next year. They are not going to have the opportunity.
That is why it is very wrong of the Government to throttle debate. Why can the House of Commons not also engage in what we sometimes call a little sober second thought that goes on in the other place? There has been some sober second thought going on right here in the House of Commons. Many people argue that we do not need another chamber for sober second thought. However, if we do not have sober second thought here, perhaps we are undercutting our arguments. If
we feel we should limit time for debate in the other place and if we limit time for debate here, how are we going to get people to look at these programs again and to perhaps change their minds?

He should use the abilities that I know he has to tell the Government that it does not make good sense to end this program on March 31. The program should run at least to the end of the year in order to give those people one last chance and a little bit of pre-warning. I would be prepared to compromise that far, but I would like to see the program continue to the end of 1990 as it is such an excellent and outstanding program. However, we are in the Opposition and we cannot have everything.
Surely, with the big majority the Government has, it could yield a little. It should not cut off debate. If the Bill must go to committee, Government Members should rise and tell us that they are going to let it be amended in committee in a way that will extend it for another six or eight months.
My constituents right across northern Ontario are absolutely irritated. Is the Government not listening to its own northern Ontario Members? It did not have a seat in the north before but now it has three seats from the north. For goodness sake, the Government should listen to its northern Ontario Members. I am sure they are speaking very eloquently. They must be pleading with the Government not to cut this program on March 31. The Government should listen to them and yield a little bit. It should not abuse its majority. That is not the atmosphere it created during the election campaign.
March 21, 1985

The Government did not tell Canada that there would be no opportunity at all for citizens to have some input. I never heard the Government say at any time that it was not going to listen to Members who were in the Opposition. I had the idea that we were going to have a new kind of Parliament. Mr. Speaker, on November 8, 1984, the Conservative Government announced a new way to tax our agricultural producers. Using misguided logic, it has decided to tackle the deficit by collecting $32.3 million in service fees from farmers, feed mill operators, seed growers, slaughterhouse operators, and others. A small slaughterhouse operator must now pay a minimum call-out fee of $125 to have a few carcasses graded. It is not hard to imagine that this cost will amount to several thousands of dollars over the period of a year.
The potato farmer in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick with an average farm will pay $13,000 to $20,000 each year for grading services. With potato farmers receiving less than the cost of production this year for their crop, this is a most unfair charge.
Seed growers are very concerned that the quality of Canada's seed stock will be compromised as more growers are forced outside the regulatory system due to increased input costs for pedigree control.

PETRO-CANADA ATTEMPT TO ACQUIRE CO-OP OUTLETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, March 18, I advised this House of protests I received from boards of several Saskatchewan co-operatives against attempts by Petro-Canada, a federal Crown Corporation, to acquire or take over co-op petroleum outlets. I wanted to know why a Crown corporation is attempting to acquire the outlets of co-ops which represent a completely Canadian-owned segment of the industry.
The Federated Co-Operative Association at its annual meeting on March 7 unanimously condemned Petro-Canada's attempt to acquire co-op outlets. The Liberal Government's national energy policy in 1980 stated:
The Government of Canada believes that the oil and gas sector is a unique case and that special measures are needed to ensure Canadian control.
March 21, 1985

1 pose the following questions. Was it the intent of the previous administration for this Crown corporation to acquire a completely Canadian-owned segment of the industry? Has Petro-Canada lost sight of its original mandate? While our very capable Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) works in co-operation with the provinces to solve the injustices of the Liberal's destructive energy policy, it is evident that it will take time for our Government to get Crown corporations under control. Mr. Speaker, police in South Africa today killed 14 people when they attempted to demonstrate in remembrance of the Sharpe-ville massacre of 25 years ago. On March 21, 1960, police opened fire on a crowd which was peacefully demonstrating against the pass laws. There were 69 people killed, including eight women and ten children, and 180 people wounded, including 31 women and 19 children. According to medical evidence, the police continued firing after the people began to flee, because while 30 shots had entered the wounded or dead from the front of their bodies, no less than 155 bullets had entered through their backs.
I ask all Hon. Members to reflect on the meaning of the Sharpeville massacre, the further slaughter of 14 people today, and the hundreds of people killed in the intervening 25 years. The same Government is in power and, in spite of minor changes, the same inhuman system of apartheid denies basic human rights to the black people of South Africa.
1 urge the Government, in conducting our foreign policy review, to remember that it was the Government of South Africa which initiated violence. I ask the Government to remember Sharpeville, to remember Nelson Mandela and others who were imprisoned for their people. I ask it to remember the 14 people who were gunned down by the police today.
Surely the time has come to take a strong stand and push for an international policy of disinvestment-

In a few hours, Mr. Speaker, Canadian men and women will be watching the
proceedings of the National Economic Conference to be held here in Ottawa.
One hundred and thirty-six participants-economic leaders from all Canadian circles-will review the economy, our heavy deficit burden and the employment situation. This economic summit is a ray of hope for the many Canadians now without jobs, without work. Time has come not to search for causes but rather to find alternate solutions and express a national consensus. Mr. Speaker, that is what Canadians expect. They want jobs, they want work, they want to live in dignity without having to ask for hand-outs from society. Such is the ultimate challenge of this weekend's conference.
There is not only one solution to all our woes, and the day-to-day reality calls for the implementation of a whole series of solutions. Canada's predicament will test our economic partners' willingness to co-operate. We must set our petty differences aside and approach the National Economic Conference with our attention riveted on the underprivileged in our society, on men, women and youths who are counting on us to find the jobs which will raise their hopes for the future.
Mr. Speaker, the 136 leaders who will get together this weekend deserve our full support in their quest for solutions.

Mr. Speaker, as a result of numerous hearings on farm tax issues in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, it has become very clear that any credit assistance program for farmers should be targeted primarily toward producers in financial distress. Some 15 per cent to 20 per cent of farmers in my home province of Manitoba, that is more than 600, are in serious financial circumstances. Therefore I strongly urge the Government to introduce a debt set-aside program in order to relieve targeted farmers of their oppressive debt load long enough for them to get back on their feet.
The Farm Credit Corporation estimates that a debt set-aside program could move more than 14,000 financially distressed Canadian farmers into a position, after five years, of having a reasonable chance of success.
I also wish to point out that more and more farmers are turning over their land to the FCC, then leasing 'it back in order to stay in business. Therefore I recommend the following: first, that these farmers be allowed to sign leases of more than one year in duration, perhaps three to five years; second, that these farmers retain the option of buying back their own land.
Canadian farmers do not want hand-outs. What they want and deserve is a little help over a very rough period.

2,000	families waiting for social housing and the list grows by 200 per month. In Toronto there are over 11,000 families waiting.
The Ontario Government has shown, by its ill-conceived housing policies, that it does not want or deserve responsibility for social housing. We need leadership from the federal Government, not delay. We want action and financing now.

Mr. Speaker, at least nine families in Canada have found a way to cope with the cost of living. They control $9 billion worth of corporate assets, or 46 per cent of the TSE 300. According to the Canadian Bankers' Association, this poses serious dangers for our financial markets. I would like to identify just a few of those dangers. It means a concentration of wealth which works against competition, and therefore against the consuming public. It means diverting human and financial resources away from the creativity and innovation our economy needs. It means at least a potential for excessive economic power as well as excessive political power. The most serious feature of all is its exponential growth.
Most of this concentration has occurred in the past 15 years. If the trend continues, Canada may find itself under a new form of the old Family Compact. Its dangerous potential has been signalled by the Canadian Bankers' Association. It is time for Parliament to alert itself. This is not a matter of right or left, of mediocrity seeking revenge against success. It is a concern about preserving competition and keeping free enterprise free.

That is why I made the suggestion that we do it without debate. I will discuss the matter with my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), and with the House Leader for the New Democratic Party immediately. We will try to get some action on this on behalf of those many, many Canadians who are affected by this important study.

subsubtopic: PRESENTATION OFSECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table in both official languages the second report of the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise in the House this afternoon to make a statement regarding
March 21, 1985

International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. As most Members know, today is the 18th anniversary of the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination which the United Nations called upon its member states to observe annually as of March 21, 1967. Canada is also supporting the second decade of action to combat racism and racial discrimination adopted by the United Nations last year.
Comparatively, Canadian society is fundamentally tolerant and accommodating of the cultural and racial diversity that has become an increasing part of our social landscape and has enriched our lives as Canadians. We should not, however, be lulled into complacency. Racial discrimination is still present in our society, as numerous studies, such as Equality Now and the Abella report on Equality in Employment, have testified. There is, therefore, a need to be ever vigilant.
Canadians are determined to eliminate this phenomenon from their midst. The coming into force of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms on equality rights on April 17, and Section 27 on the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians, are major steps that will afford better protection to minorities, including cultural and racial minorities.
The Government is committed to creating a climate of mutual tolerance among Canadians so that all of us, irrespective of our racial or ethnic origins, can contribute to and participate fully and equally in the life of our country for the benefit of all of our society. This commitment is clearly demonstrated by the number of major initiatives which we have undertaken in response to both the Abella and Equality Now reports.
The Government's positive response to the Abella report is a major step toward eliminating racial discrimination in federally-regulated employment. For example, visible minorities will for the first time be a target group for employment equity in the federal sector. That is a major breakthrough, since employment is such a critical part of life in our society.
The current deliberations of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission in the report entitled A Proposal for an Ethnic Broadcasting Policy for Canada will certainly reinforce the multicultural fabric of our nation.
The Government will also work co-operatively with other jurisdictions to eliminate discrimination. The Government is sponsoring the first Federal-Provincial-Territorial Conference on Multiculturalism, which will he held this May. That conference will explore how this co-operation can best be achieved. We are also discussing with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities what new initiatives can be undertaken to address the issue of racial discrimination at the municipal level.
Last October, Multiculturalism Canada and the Canadian Association of Police Chiefs co-sponsored a successful national symposium on policing in multicultural-multiracial urban communities. As a result, the association is making this the
Elimination of Racial Discrimination theme of its next annual conference, which will be held later this year, as part of its follow-up commitment.
In addition, we will continue to develop further new initiatives in a number of social areas that will make Canadians and their institutions open and equitable for all citizens, irrespective of their racial, ethnic or cultural backgrounds.
Canadians are realizing that Canada has become a culturally and racially diverse nation, populated by talented and capable people from all parts of the world. The people of a nation are its most important resource. The richness of our diversity is certainly our greatest asset which, allowed to flourish to its fullest potential, can benefit us all.
Canada as a nation has an enviable reputation in the world of which we can all be proud. Let us all work together to make it better.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by thanking the Minister for giving us an advance copy of his statement. He will know that a week ago I was critical of one of his colleagues because I did not receive that statement in advance. I want to give credit where credit is due. As the Minister knows, providing advance copies permits members of the Opposition to comment more constructively and with more meaning on these statements.
I would also like to thank the Minister for making this statement in the House. By doing that, he gives the House of Commons an opportunity to make pronouncements on very important matters and to state before the Canadian people that this House is against all kinds of discrimination, especially racial discrimination.
Hear, hear!

It is very important for all of us to show leadership in this respect. As the Minister pointed out in his statement, although much progress has been made in this country, problems still exist. Last year in the City of Montreal there was a serious problem with respect to our black taxi drivers, and a commission was set up by the provincial Government to deal with that problem. I also raised in this House the problem of a young black man who was refused entrance to a cafe in the City of Montreal. Problems still exist, and we must be ever-vigilant in dealing with those problems.
There have been countries in which great progress has been made. However, during times of unemployment and other crises there is always the tendency for this ugly side of humanity to express itself, and consequently we must forever work on these matters.
Today the Minister has principally dealt with racial discrimination. However, there are many other kinds of discrimination which are just as odious-religious, ethnic, linguistic, sexual and the discrimination against the handicapped. Recently in Canada we saw the terrible experiences of the Zundel trial and the Keegstra case in the west in which

March 21, 1985
Elimination of Racial Discrimination
discrimination was expressed against our Jewish brothers. Together we must bring in amendments to the Criminal Code with respect to hate literature. Also, during the last election campaign I noticed a backlash against some of our immigrant groups in Canada, especially the Asian and black people. I am afraid that there are still issues of linguistic discrimination for minorities in the Province of Quebec, and francophone minorities in other parts of the country.
Those of us who have been at the hearings of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development over the last couple of weeks when it has been discussing Bill C-31 will know of the many sad stories which were put before that committee. It gives us a real education regarding the discrimination which exists against Indian and native people in the country. If there is one area where there is a major problem, it is in the discrimination which is practised against many of our Indian and native people. When we visit our large cities and see the ghettos in which Indian people live and the problems that they have with employment and many other matters, it is obvious that that is one of the principal areas in which we must take action, whether it be in housing, education or other areas.
The Equality Now report to which the Minister referred was a major report of the last Parliament. It was a unanimous report of all Parties of the House. It was tabled a year ago with 80 recommendations. I am pleased to see that we are now beginning to move ahead to implement those recommendations.
It is interesting to note that in the last Parliament there were several committees and commissions which dealt with discrimination. The Obstacles report dealt with problems of the handicapped and the Equality Now report dealt with problems of visible minorities. The Special Committee which I chaired on Employment Opportunities for the '80s dealt with the problems of minority groups. Chapter 11 of the report dealt with employment problems.
When the Government announced its response to the Abella report last week, I indicated that we were pleased with certain of the proposals which were definitely moves in the right direction. However, we were concerned by the lack of an enforcement agency and sanctions. We were also concerned that the contract compliance provisions would only apply to 100 out of approximately 30,000 businesses which deal with the Government. We were also concerned that the proposals would only apply to 800 out of approximately 4,500 federally-regulated firms. Nevertheless, these are moves in the right direction and we will watch closely to see what happens with respect to the measures which have been announced by the Government.
Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms comes into effect on April 17. That will be a landmark-
I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member, but I am afraid that his time has expired, unless the House will grant its unanimous consent for him to continue.
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to say that Section 15 has great significance because it will apply to all federal and provincial legislation. It will override any provincial or federal law which contains discrimination with respect to the target groups, including the visible minorities, women, senior citizens and so on. In his statement the Minister said that he would take action to get the provinces to comply in these matters. That is very important, because the federal Government only covers a small area of the total field.
I want to assure the Minister that we in this Party will give our full support in moving ahead in the fight against racial discrimination. The Minister will find that we will be behind any legislation which he introduces in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with my colleagues in recognizing the statement which was made today. Although this statement deals only with discrimination as it exists in Canada, I think we must recognize that we in Canada have a responsibility regarding discrimination in other parts of the world. We have to be ever vigilant against the tendency among those who would discriminate to force their will on what are frequently the minorities in other countries. It is unfortunate that we continually have to raise the problem of discrimination. That discrimination is not dead either here in Canada or in other countries around the world. It continues to rear its ugly head. It is only by virtue of these problems being constantly raised and by virtue of discussions we have inside and outside of this Parliament about discrimination which is practised not only in Canada but in other parts of the world, that we are able to cause those who would discriminate to jactitation.
It is important that we make those who would discriminate very nervous about their tendency and proclivity to cause harm to others who are perhaps unable to speak for themselves. Just today, for example, my colleague raised the situation in South Africa where 14 people were shot to death on the anniversary not only of the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination but on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre. These 14 people were shot to death because they stood up against discrimination.
I want to say that this Parliament has an obligation to make known to the Governments of those countries with which we do business and which rely on us in many ways for the continuance of their economic well-being, that we will not sit idly by and watch while they undertake the kinds of measures which caused those 14 deaths. That applies not only to South Africa but to many other parts of the world. It applies, as Hon. Members will know, to the Soviet Union where we frequently find there is a measure of discrimination taken against individuals, particularly because of their religious beliefs, but not always.
As we recognize the day, we must also recognize not only the marginal successes-and there have been some-but the terrible failures. Although we stand up and say that this is an important day, the real importance of it will be measured only
March 21, 1985

when we can look inside and outside our country and see that the ugly head of discrimination has finally vanished from the international scene.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his comments the Minister reminded the House that racial discrimination still exists in Canada, and that we must try, with the co-operation of various agencies, to remove and extirpate this cancer from our society.
I would like to ask the Minister the following question. Since the previous Government had a program to help people who felt their rights had been infringed upon, a legal aid program that provided financial assistance to people who wanted to take legal action to defend their rights before the courts, could the Minister inform the House whether, when he says that we are determined to wipe out this phenomenon, and considering the fact that Section 15 of the Constitution comes into effect on April 17, and that this section is directly concerned with the subject, he is prepared to recommend to Cabinet that the legal aid program be expanded to cover racial discrimination?

Mr. Speaker, that is a good question. It is certainly something which has been contemplated in the minds of many people in this country. I would think-and once again, I am not a lawyer-that given what most people expect to be an increased work load which will very likely be undertaken, some form of compensation or help will have to be looked at and considered by Parliament at some point in time.

Mr. Speaker, not only are there problems of discrimination and racism which we attempt to deal with in Canada, but there are problems beyond the borders of Canada. In fact, the way we act often times carries a much more impressive message than the way we talk. I wonder if the Minister is prepared to look at some of our relationships with particular countries which practise, as part of their Constitution, racism and discrimination? I am referring to South Africa. Is the Minister prepared to use his influence within the Cabinet to make sure, for example, that South African Krugerrand gold coins are not imported into Canada and sold through Canadian banks to Canadian entrepreneurs?

Mr. Speaker, that question, I suppose, stretches the jurisdiction in terms of our discussion this afternoon. Certainly, the Cabinet itself, the Government and the House of Commons will want to do everything in their power to make sure that we are not only viewed properly outside of our country-which means, of course, cleaning up our own act; people are watching us from that point of view-but that we also show the world that we mean business in our outside dealings. I feel certain that Canada is well regarded in this area. The Hon. Member's comments will be taken into consideration. It is something with which certainly the Government itself would have to deal. At the present time, however, there is no indication that that will take place.
Elimination of Racial Discrimination

Mr. Speaker, this past week there was a story in the press about a hotel in Prince George where one of the people working in that hotel indicated there was a policy of refusing entrance to all of the Indian people from a certain Indian band in northern British Columbia. I understant that there has since been an official retraction but I suspect that this is really just the tip of the iceberg. This is a situation which pops up every now and again and we become aware of the kind of systemic discrimination which often takes place against Indian people in many communities across Canada.
Would the Minister undertake an investigation into the situation at Prince George in order to make sure that Indian people are not discriminated against when they try to get accommodation in that city?

Mr. Speaker, the matter raised by the Hon. Member is an important one. It also, I suspect, falls somewhat within the provincial jurisdiction. Nevertheless, we are concerned that there is discrimination in any part of Canada and anything we as a Government can do to help the minorities in this country who are discriminated against-and certainly Indian people fall right within that category-we will endeavour to do.
Our whole thrust in acting as quickly as we have on the Abella Commission report, which deals primarily with native groups, women's groups, the handicapped and visible minorities, is to ensure that when we go out to support a group of people which have suffered discrimination, we will have something there to talk about; that we as a Government in effect have cleaned up our act. Only then, in my opinion, can we go out and point the finger at various groups of people. We are very sensitive and concerned about the issue and 1 will endeavour to get as much information on it as I can.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to join my colleagues in congratulating the Minister on his statement. I think his declaration in principle . . . We are all for virtue and motherhood, but on page 2 of his statement, he again refers to the coming into effect on April 17 of Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I would like to elaborate on what my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) said about legal recourse.
The House is aware that the coming into effect of this section of our new Constitution is very significant for the enforcement of certain kinds of legislation. We know that, usually, victims of discrimination belong to minorities that, unfortunately, have too little clout. And now that the coming into effect of Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is imminent, could the Minister give the House the assurance that when Section 15 becomes effective, we will know whether he is prepared to put his money where his mouth is and ensure that, as he said earlier, the rights and freedoms of individuals are truly protected and that the legis-

March 21, 1985
Elimination of Racial Discrimination lation is not just a piece of paper but a living reality for those Canadians who need this kind of protection?
To get back to the question put by my hon. colleague, we do not want to know whether there will be a program in a month of Sundays. What we want to know is whether, when the Bill receives royal assent, the Minister is going to put his money where his mouth is and ensure that a properly financed legal aid program will put some teeth into Section 15 of the Charter.

Mr. Speaker, that question would have been better directed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) because he is going to be the man dealing with this particular area. As the Hon. Member knows, the Minister of Justice has set up a select committee to study the charter and its implications. Of course, that will be something this committee will be dealing with.
To get directly to the Hon. Member's question, it is not practical, shall we say. We can all imagine the work load, because of the coming into effect of the charter, through a buildup of many different types of cases. None of us can envisage that without some assistance at some point in time, and certainly the Government will be looking at that, as I hope the Opposition and the committee itself will do, and the recommendations we receive will be dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, in 1979 the UN Assembly designated the week beginning March 21 as the week of solidarity with people struggling against racism and racial discrimination. Indeed, today is the day that the City of Ottawa declared as the international day for the elimination of racial discrimination. So my question to the Minister is very specific and once again deals with our performance and something which gives us credibility not only in Canada but also outside Canada, that being the code of behaviour for Canadian companies operating in South Africa.
These companies are supposed to file an accountability report on their compliance with that code of behaviour. As far as 1 know, Alcan is the only company which has filed that annual report since it was instituted. Can the Minister promise this House that he will at least go back to Cabinet and demand that Canadian companies like Bata Shoe and Falconbridge comply with that minimum standard of behaviour for which we ask?
Which is required.
Yes, it is required.

Mr. Speaker, my Cabinet colleagues involved in this particular matter, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher), for example, and others are aware of this. We are in the process of monitoring the companies based on the work they do and how they deal with the conditions within South Africa.
They are not monitoring very well.
As the Member knows, this is a very difficult situation.
How?
Canadian companies-it is a difficult situation within South Africa.
For them to file?
We are watching the situation and monitoring it.
People are watching you.

I am sure that the Hon. Member will be satisfied with the outcome of the process which is taking place.
[ Translation]

I must say I felt considerable concern when the Minister mentioned that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) had a committee that was dealing with the legal aid program. Since his Ministry comes under the Department of the Secretary of State, Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister ought to know that at least in the past, the Secretary of State has always been responsible for the legal aid program, and there was no screening by the Department of Justice with respect to this program. Did the Minister mean to say that authority over the legal aid program has been transferred from the Secretary of State, who is supposed to represent minorities in Cabinet, and relegated by the Minister, now that he has lost his authority over the program, to officials at the Department of Justice-is that what he is telling me?

No, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry if I misinterpreted the hon. gentleman's earlier question. The heart and soul, as he says, of the protection of minorities in this country is now, always has been and always will be in the Secretary of State's Department. I can only tell the hon. gentleman that certainly if financial assistance is necessary-and we all expect it will be although only time will tell-the Government will deal with it in the most appropriate way possible in view of the fact that we are dealing with a very sensitive matter which involves minority rights and minorities across this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by students of Laval University asking for a change in the government economic policy.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise (for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works; and the motion of Mr. Hockin (p. 3227).
Oil Substitution Act

subtopic: OIL SUBSTITUTION AND CONSERVATION ACT CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise again in this debate. Yesterday 1 had an opportunity to urge the House to consider the possibility of allowing a six-month delay before Bill C-24 becomes law. Unfortunately, the way things are this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, parliamentarians have a sword of Damocles hanging over their heads, and once again we must conclude that tyranny by the majority prevents us from properly debating this measure.
In view of their overwhelming majority, Mr. Speaker, our colleagues opposite have decided once again to gag us, to impose closure on a Bill which is of vital importance to many Canadian families. Not only did they choose to drop a program which is very important in many localities in Canada- in mid-November to boot-but they also sprang this announcement on us without notice. They are now intent on preventing the House of Commons from giving due consideration to this Bill which concerns many families in all ridings.
Sure enough, the Government did not pay much attention to our speeches so far, and no amendment is forthcoming to make sure that the Canadian Oil Substitution Program will be extended until some time in September or October instead of ending on March 31. Mr. Speaker, when the Government is primarily concerned about the fact that March 31 marks the end of the fiscal year, we seriously wonder just why it announced in the middle of November that March 31 will be the end of a program which directly involves the construction industry as well as electrical and home heating contractors.
Mr. Speaker, you will certainly agree that if you were planning to replace your furnace, you would not do it in the middle of February. If you were planning to convert to natural gas, it is not at this time, when the ground is still frozen, that gas lines would be installed.
The people who are supposed to have all the answers therefore did not realize that, by cancelling a program in the middle of winter, they would prevent Canadian men and women who wished to use the oil conversion program to do so and would take away for all practical purposes, their opportunity to use the program.
During the debate, I heard many Members say that people have known of this deadline since November. I am pleased to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) among us since he is supposed to care about what happens to the poor in Canada. Since the grant did not cover 100 per cent of conversion costs, the Minister should realize that many families could not, in such a short time, put aside the money needed to undertake such a project. Many families could not afford to undertake immediately a project which could cost thousands of dollars. The word discrimination was mentioned a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-24 indeed discriminates against all those who were unable to save enough money between November and today to undertake conversion work in

March 21, 1985
Oil Substitution Act
their homes, and it is also discriminatory to provide so little time until the deadline, especially since the public was convinced that the program would be maintained until December 31, 1990. Because of this, I know of many people who had planned major renovations in their homes for next summer, but who were waiting until then to convert their heating system and stop being dependent on oil.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the situation is about the same in the Temiscamingue (Mr. Desjardins), and I am convinced that the situation is about the same in the Temiscamingue constituency. I can see the Hon. Member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Desjardins), and I am convinced that there are families with the same problems in his riding. It is quite cold in that region, and I am certain that very few people converted their heating system in February or March of this year. All these people will therefore be unable to apply under the oil substitution program.
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter for concern since natural gas has just become available in certain regions. And we know how people are unwilling to accept changes. Those people who have just become users of natural gas-and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) who is in this House, will confirm that many areas of Canada and especially Quebec have just been connected with the natural gas system and that her department's interest in helping to finance the laying of natural gas branch lines was of course to have industrial conversions. But her department was certainly expecting several residential conversions. Instead of slashing the program, the Minister should realize that such conversions could not be carried out during the winter. She should know of course that the ground is frozen hard in most parts of Canada, except perhaps in Vancouver, Mr. Speaker. But in all other regions, and certainly the Minister knows the situation in the Eastern Townships, for instance, because she herself has provided money for the installation of natural gas branch lines, she should realize that there was not enough time for people to make the conversion, that her announcement implied in the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) came too late, and that the entire construction industry, the electricians and the natural gas people, are asking that the program's termination date be changed.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of reasons for requesting such an extension. By creating as she did an emergency situation, the Minister has actually caused what is called a shortage of equipment in many remote areas of Canada, where equipment can only be shipped by boat.

speechtext: It is a money shortage.
