speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear the Minister say it is a money shortage. She is a Member of Cabinet and she lets her colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) spend $56 million on army uniforms. The Minister should be ashamed of referring to a shortage of money. When she lets
the Minister of National Defence buy planes, at $10 million a piece, for her to travel around she should be ashamed! And if she has no power in Cabinet, if she does not have enough clout to save her department's money, she should not come in this House and try to insult Opposition Members who have concern for Canadians, Mr. Speaker.
I am happy to see the Minister here, because we are going to tell her what the people in our constituencies think. Our constituents are saying that the Minister knows nothing about construction, that she does not know that a heating system is not to be converted during the winter, that she does not know that we have just been provided with natural gas. But this is what we want her to hear today. And I am pleased, because Hon. Members in her own party do not look as though they were going to tell her. Since I have been listening to this debate, Mr. Speaker, very few Conservative Members have participated. They will not have me believe that the situation in their constituencies is any different from what it is in ours. They will not convince me for instance that the CHIP Program in their constituencies is having less success than elsewhere.
She is also talking about terminating the Canadian Home Insulation Program next year. A program that has met with an interesting success, for which her department had set a goal of 5 million homes. Now this program is halfway through, with 2.5 million homes that have been insulated. Does she intend to convince me that all of the other 2.5 million homes will be insulated in the coming year? I would like to believe that, Mr. Speaker, but I feel she is deluding herself. To that extent, it is amazing how far the Government will go in the way of cheese-paring. That program allowed thousands of Canadian home owners to conserve energy. Is there anything wrong with Canadian men and women conserving energy? It has helped us reduce our oil dependency. And it is an illusion to think that because there has been a slight decrease in the price of oil, this will last forever. I believe Canada cannot afford to depend too much on any form of energy. And the diversification effected by the program was precisely intended to reduce Canadian dependency on any one form, or a number of forms of energy. And in that sense ... I see that my friend from Champlain (Mr. Champagne) is arriving. I am sure that he will tell you, Mr. Speaker, about the negative effects his riding will get because this program is cut off. I am sure that he will refer to the electrical contractors, the plumbers and the people installing heating systems who tell him that it is senseless to cut it off in the middle of March because it is in the spring and in summer that construction is carried on in the constituency of Champlain. It is only in the constituency of the Minister that the work can be carried throughout the year, Mr. Speaker. This is the reason why she may not understand the ill effects of those cuts. Now the government has decided to muzzle the Members-
March 21, 1985

Mr. Speaker, you are telling me that the time allotted to me is unfortunately expired. I could have told you about the negative effects of the unilateral decision taken by the Minister but unfortunately due to the callousness of that government and because of closure, I am unable to continue my remarks on such an important issue.

subtopic: OIL SUBSTITUTION AND CONSERVATION ACT CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak briefly on Bill C-24. At the beginning of my remarks I would like to express a certain degree of frustration with the way in which things are going. On the one hand, there seems to be a great deal of publicity and media attention given to the Prime Minister's meeting with President Reagan which accomplished very little for the Canadian people. On the other hand, we are here debating cut-backs that are of basic importance to thousands of Canadians across the country and it seems that it is being done almost in a vacuum.
This Government seems very successful in one respect in that it is accomplishing media events. It does not seem to be directing its energy toward tackling the fundamental problems of our economy. When it does address the economy, it usually does so in a backward move.
We have to ask why the Government is taking such a penny-wise, pound-foolish approach to the economy. The Government ostensibly gives the reason that it wants to cut back on the deficit and that is why the Government is cutting programs like this one which, as Members opposite acknowledge, have performed a useful function over the last few years. The Tories acknowledge they have been good programs and have helped Canadians. Yet the Tories cut these programs because they say they are concerned about the deficit. If they are so concerned about the deficit, Mr. Speaker, I wish they were a little more careful about the way they use government executive jets. It was reported in the news paper last week that some Cabinet Minister had to fly to Vancouver on a jet at a cost of $19,000. We have, on the one hand, this kind of extravagance and waste and, on the other hand, we are cutting back on programs that will affect the well-being of the ordinary people.
We can look at the issue that was brought up by one of my colleagues, the question of changing lawyers for the Farm Credit Corporation. In spite of the answer given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) today, there will be a training period required, and this will be a further expense.
We see the Government cutting programs of demonstrated value. In addition to the two we are talking about today, I can cite such programs as the fishermen's insurance, which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) brought up today, or the cuts in the residential rehabilitation assistance program.
The programs we are talking about today covered by Bill C-24, involve oil substitution and the Canadian Home Insulation Program. These programs have been fundamentally
Oil Substitution Act
beneficial to Canadians and have helped the economy. I would like to suggest at least three ways in which these programs have been helpful.
First, they have reduced our consumption of oil. As we all should know, oil is a finite resource. The National Energy Board has estimated that by the year 2005 our production of conventional crude will be about 28 per cent of what it is today.
Second, these programs have provided jobs all across Canada. They have provided jobs for people involved in insulation and retrofitting.
Third, these programs have benefited the economy because they has enabled home owners to save on their heating bills.
It is important to stress that when the home owner is able to save a little bit of money and when money is tight in most households, that money will go into other sections of the economy. The money will keep circulating rather than going to the oil companies.
These programs are popular. The Canadian Oil Substitution Program is now halfway through its projected mandate. It was supposed to run to 1990. It is more or less on target in terms of its projection, but instead it will be terminated at the end of March. It is interesting that the gas contracting firms are complaining now about the haste with which COSP has been terminated and the waste this creates because a lot of people have been trying to get in under the deadline in order to take advantage of the program. People have made applications and the gas companies have been trying to put in lines in the middle of the winter, a most costly and wasteful approach. At the very least the Government could have given a little more notice. That was the substance of the motion we moved last week when we asked the Government to give the Bill an extra six-month consideration.
On Vancouver Island people suffer a double penalty. This has been pointed out before. People on Vancouver Island were not able to take advantage of the program until 1983 because there was a lot of thought that a natural gas pipeline would be built to the Island. When the program first came into effect, it was put on hold after a few weeks, and it was not until 1983 that people were able to take advantage of COSP when they went of oil to electricity or to wood stoves, or whatever.
It has been reported that by helping people to move off oil COSP has saved 15.3 million a barrels of oil a year, enough oil to heat 650,000 homes. Between 1981 and 1985 COSP provided 16,750 jobs. Now when we have 1.5 million people unemployed, perhaps the Government thinks that over 16,000 jobs is not very much and it can just forget about them. Every job is important.
The same is true for CHIP. Between 1977 and 1982 some
44,000	person-years of work were created by the program. The Oil Substitution Program was able to provide some 30.5 person-years for every $1 million invested. The Government is going ahead with these cuts, and we have to ask why. Before the election we never heard anything about this. Since the Government has been elected, we have not heard jobs, jobs, jobs, but cut-back, cut-back, cut-back. This last week we have heard just one word and that one word is "unde", Mr. Speaker. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 trust the House realizes that the Official Opposition's decision to oppose Bill C-24 was not made because we enjoy this kind of debate. We have very serious reasons for opposing the Bill, because we believe that the Government's approach to this matter is entirely unreasonable. 1 would like to elaborate, for your benefit and for the benefit of Government Members present, on our three reasons for opposing the Bill. First of all, we think the Bill is absolutely unfair because it means changing the rules of the game while the players are still on the ice, to draw a parallel with the sports world. It is exactly that.
Second, there are large regions that have not been able to take advantage of the oil substitution and insulation programs. I am thinking, for instance, of the area around Quebec City and the towns of Charlesbourg and Beauport. I will get back to this later on.
Finally, my third reason for rising in the House today is the fact that this Government, for the second time in its short existence, a Government with a majority of 211 Members against 80, even less than 80 on the Opposition side, is using closure, is gagging debate.

Since the November announcement of the demise of COSP, many consumers have been scrambling to take advantage of it before the March 31, 1985 deadline. Using the example of Consumers Gas of Ontario, I will try to illustrate the fact that gas companies are faced with enormous problems because of increased demand and the short time between the time when they received notice and the deadline. For fiscal year October 1, 1983 to February 28, 1984, Consumers Gas received close to 5,000 applications for conversions to natural gas. In the period from October 1, 1984 to February 26, 1985, it received close to 18,000 applications, of which 9,000 were made in January and February. Faced with this amount of demand, the industry cannot possibly install these systems by the March 31 deadline. This means that on April Fool's Day, a tremendous number of consumers will be left holding the bag.
There are many reasons the industry is having problems serving home owners. One reason is weather. It is extremely difficult to install gas pipelines when trying to dig through snow-covered ground. The problem in northern Ontario is even worse. Northern and Central Gas Corporation Ltd. stopped taking applications in December because it could not break through the frost-covered ground. The Canadian Gas Association approached the Government asking for an extension, as has Consumers Gas and other interested parties, and was turned down. Many solutions were proposed. It volunteered to cut off program applications at the end of January, as long as the Government gave companies and the home owners time to install all systems, but that was also turned down.
The bottom line is that the Government wants to cut off the money, no matter how many people want to convert to gas. The industry does not really mind, and perhaps some people in Canada would accept the cut-off of this program, but they would like it to be done in a more normal way. A phase-out is absolutely essential.

Mr. Speaker, there are certainly problems in Northern Ontario and elsewhere in Canada, but nowhere are they felt as acutely as in the province of Quebec. And I refer to the situation which exists in Quebec City and within the Greater Quebec City area, since not a single hon. member from the Progressive Conservative Party seems to be concerned about it.
Last November, this government announced two decisions which have greatly affected in a negative way the Greater Quebec City area. First it announced that it had cancelled all plans for the then forthcoming construction of branch lines to the natural gas pipe-line, affecting negatively the cities of Charlesbourg and Beauport, and also the Lauzon area and especially the Lauzon Point which could eventually be used for the development of an industrial complex. But to return to this program, not only were the Beauport and Charlesbourg area deprived of investments which would have enabled the industrial park and the residents of these densely populated cities to have access to natural gas, but also the plans for the industrial development which the construction of these branch lines would have made possible were aborted.
I have met personally the spokesmen for the Metro-Quebec Chamber of Commerce and this is one of the problems that were brought to our attention, that have been under consideration and the disposition of which was overdue. I am referring for instance to the establishment of a separate board of directors for the airport and to the upgrading of the Quebec-Montreal railway lines.
But coming back to the matter now under consideration, these areas of Charlesbourg and Beauport and eventually Lauzon are being denied the opportunity to benefit from the program. This legislation is suddenly cutting out homeowners not only in the areas already served, but also in areas which could not make use of the program because natural gas had
March 21, 1985

not been available, and they are denied a program that has been used by a number of Canadians. In my view, that decision is seriously affecting citizens in the Metro-Quebec area, not to mention of course, as I said earlier, that the guillotine will fall on March 31. This means that many people, many families will not have an opportunity to avail themselves of the positive benefits of the program, the value of which has been recognized by all Hon. Members in this House.
The third reason why I am taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is the guillotine being imposed upon this House. It is beyond me that this Government, which has been boasting ever since September 4 that it wanted to consult and listen to everybody before taking decisions, is refusing to do it here in this House. And when the Opposition becomes insistant, there is a short period of patience and immediately the guillotine falls. Even though I was sitting in this House before, I often listened to the debates and watched them on television. An I remember how the Government Members of today used to behave when the previous Government used that procedure or talked of using it to end debate, at a time when the House of Commons was more evenly balanced between Government and Opposition parties. Today, using guillotine when there is a mere handful of Opposition members, when that same Government talks about wanting to consult, when it says it is ready to spend huge sums of money on economic summits-Hurray for economic summits! So much the better if they want to listen to people from across the border! But why will they not listen to Members in this House who are trying to have the Minister understand why it makes no sense to suddenly, without notice, without a warning period, terminate such a program, and on top of that to use the guillotine to deny the benefits of a program whose value for the people and for better use of energy in Canada has been recognized by everyone?
Mr. Speaker, I wish and I hope that after hearing the same arguments, even repeatedly, at some point somebody on the Government side will see the light and accept to bring in amendments to the legislation now before us.

Under normal circumstances, I probably would have considered that participation to be sufficient. I confess, unashamedly, that we are attempting to stall the Bill. We are not asking for an unlimited extension. We are not asking that the law be extended ad infinitum. We are suggesting that because of the timing of the Government's move to limit access to this program, it has made it impossible for a significantly large number of Canadians, who otherwise would have taken advantage of the opportunity to be assisted in the financing of what most believe is worth-while work, both from the point of view of employment and from the point of view of energy savings, to access this program.

speechtext: We would have to borrow the money.

The Minister says to me quietly across the floor that the Government would have to borrow the money. I can well appreciate that that would be a view that the Cabinet would put forward. This shows that, as a priority matter, this falls considerably far down the list of priorities of the Government. This is a statement that I find, although understandably coming from the Conservative administration, unacceptable from the point of view of what will be best in the over-all for the country as a whole.
Let me suggest to the Minister that many of those people who will not now be able to access this program have had their

tax dollars used to allow others to take advantage of it. Because of the way this has been terminated and the time of the year-and I am trying truthfully to look at it-the termination date makes it virtually impossible for a large number of Canadians to be able to take advantage of what was intended to be available to all.
I suggest to the Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that one need not be a genius-I do not pretend to be and, 1 am sure, neither does the Minister-to see that it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, for work to be done in some areas of the country over the winter. During the months from November through until the end of March, which was the period for winding down or winding up, depending on your choice, the program that we are now debating, it was absolutely impossible, with all of the best intentions in the world, for many people to get into the program and take advantage of it. There is clear evidence to show that there are a large number of people who would still like to use it.
I have to say that at first I was somewhat puzzled by the Government's attitude. This is a Government that, as I said the other day, has elevated simony to an art form. It has redefined it in the political context. Again today we were able to see further examples of how this Government can find jobs for its friends, regardless of where those friends are, all of those jobs to be paid for out of the public purse, and yet the Government cannot seem to find the will to reapportion some resources to allow citizens of Canada access to a program that not only benefits them personally, but benefits many who are unemployed in the country. It will benefit the country in the longer run in terms of our judicious use of our energy resources.
What we are saying, quite bluntly, is that from our point of view, it would be better if the Government were to be less generous in a partisan hack way with the resources of the country and somewhat more understanding of the benefits that could be derived from the continuation of this program for a short period of time. As I said yesterday, that period of time could be until the middle of the fall. That would allow for proper planning. It would allow people to make arrangements for whatever additional funding they require. It would enable the companies involved to plan for employment during a period when there will be a number of people unemployed due to the termination of the program. It would give time for the Government's new economic program which it is going to unveil some time between now and June to take effect. It would afford many an opportunity to access the new employment program that the Government continues to tell us it is prepared to make available.
In the over-all, the request that we make is a reasonable and fair request. We are not asking that the program be extended forever. We are asking that the program be extended into the summer months in order to allow those who would want to take advantage of it to be able to complete what they believe they would be able to complete if it were not for the weather.
Let us not base our judgment solely on what can be done in southern Ontario. I come from southern Ontario, but southern
Ontario is not all of Canada. There are many parts of Canada where the work we are talking about could not have been undertaken between the months of November and April.
I do not think it is unreasonable to suggest something like that. Those people have been asked to contribute out of their tax dollars to provide the benefits and the savings to others in the country. We should ensure that they too are given a chance to take advantage of that program, given the chance to do so with an understanding that the program will in fact come to an end, but it will come to an end at such a time as to guarantee that they could, if they wished, access the program for their own benefit and for the benefit of others who might work in the program.
It is no wonder, as I look across the floor of the House, that I feel a sort of sense of twitchiness on the government backbenches and the evidence of jactitation on the government benches. Quite clearly, the government Members recognize the merit of the position that we are putting forward. I can see evidence among the few that are here that they would like to see the Government undertake to provide the extension that we are asking for.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation

The one thing the Government has demonstrated in the last six months is its ability to be unfair. It has been unfair in the way in which it made cuts in its November economic statement, cuts which detrimentally affected so many people and were made without consultation. It has been unfair in the way in which it went about setting up an economic conference after it made decisions about what would be contained in the Budget. It has been unfair about its presentation of the unfortunate incidents that occurred in Ottawa just one week ago. Some day the Government must recognize that, in a representative system, it is imperative that the Government show complete fairness.
Fairness is not simply exemplified by appointing friends to high offices at high costs. Fairness is exemplified by treating Canadians in such a way that they feel they are being considered. They are not being considered by the termination of this program. I would simply suggest that we give it another six months or even five months. We should give it a little more time in order to give people a chance to do what they would otherwise do to help the economic stability for which we are all looking.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise as other members who have preceded me, to speak on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act.
March 21, 1985

However, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of what we have heard so far, from both sides of the House, it would seem that the two programs I mentioned earlier and which are dealt with in Bill C-24, are viewed as satisfactory by almost everyone. And rightly so, Mr. Speaker! The reason for this is quite simple. If we look at a map, we can see that Canada is a country located in the Northern part of America. Our country is quite cold, and as people often say, there are two seasons in Canada, the month of July and winter. Naturally, to make our houses and work places comfortable, it is essential to have adequate heating.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that Canada has suffered a lot, especially since the energy world crisis of the 70's which caused great economic upheaval in industrialized countries because of the rapid increase in the price of oil, but the worst is now over.
Our problems have many causes. First of all, in the past, Canadian houses were built with two by fours or two by sixes with sawdust between the walls as insulation. This did not make the houses very warm. There was much more humidity and cold than anything else. In addition, it was very costly. However, since oil then cost between 11 and 15 cents a gallon, people still had no reason to complain or to find the cost excessive. But after the crisis of the 70's, we had to review our position. We had to develop programs so that Canadians would have comfortable well-heated houses because, as I said earlier, we have two seasons, winter and the month of July. Programs were therefore developed to conserve as much energy as possible so that Canadians would be warm and able to work and live comfortably and decently in spite of our northern climate.
I heard the Minister say in a recent speech that energy conservation was like a new energy source. She was right. I agree wholeheartedly with her because this is an inexhaustible source of energy. Thanks to the programs which have been implemented over the last few years, it is estimated that we have been able to save 82,000 barrels of oil a day. It is also estimated that about 2.5 million housing units have been insulated through CHIPS. Of course, this program must disappear eventually, but in my opinion, the Government acted somewhat irresponsibly when it announced last November 8 that all work would have to be completed by March 31. I do not want to repeat once more that it is rather difficult to change or convert a heating system-

If we extended it until June, so that those who are first time home purchasers, not new houses because most new houses now have the necessary equipment to prevent heat losses, but an older house . . . those who are getting married for the first time, who are first time purchasers of older houses not fitted with proper insulation and the necessary equipment for proper heating, I feel that we should make it possible for them to benefit from this program. Eventually, when all the tests have been completed for projects such as the R-2,000 model house built by Mortgage and Housing Canada, I think then perhaps these programs could be reduced.
As long as there are home owners who have not availed themselves of these programs, Mr. Speaker, we should maintain them, for they play a major role in conserving energy. I know there are other means but it is one of those which will help achieve energy self-sufficiency for Canada. Because Canadians live in a part of the North American continent where winters can be very cold and with a nearly Arctic climate, the Government should make cuts where they are not likely to jeopardize the health and comfort of Canadians.
Cuts have to be made, Mr. Speaker, but not necessarily where savings ... at least not in the building industry, for the jobs of many electricians and heating technicians are at stake. Because such an action would create much unemployment, 1 do not think this is the way the government should go about it. I know that because we have this new government, people have changed. We should do things differently. I think it would be responsible also to make cuts where they are likely to improve the government's lot.
I am surprised that, practically overnight, the Government announced the abolition of those programs which all Canadians found very useful. More signficant still, they went a long way towards making Canada self-sufficient by giving us means to conserve energy and find new sources, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) so aptly put it.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker. I wish the program could be extended much later than March 31, much later than in the fall, really. However, if it has to be done this way, let us find ways to exempt or retain the program for those who need it most, low-income families that cannot at this time take advantage of benefits offered to other Canadians. All Canadians should be able to enjoy the same

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-24, which is an effort by the Government to save money. I would like to spend some time talking about the choices which have been made and the direction in which this Government seems to be going.
In an effort to save tax dollars, the Government has chosen to cut COSP, which was to have existed for ten years, until 1990. The program was designed to encourage Canadians to save on their expenditures for energy. That cost-saving measure is now being abandoned. The program also had larger energy conservation connotations, which I believe are extremely important.
In particular, COSP was designed to shift Canadian home owners from oil to other modes of energy, and in particular natural gas. It has been determined by the National Energy Board that there is a surplus of natural gas, but there is not a surplus of oil, particularly the kind of oil which is used in making diesel and fuel oil. The lighter kinds of crude are expected to produce only about 28 per cent of the current levels by the year 2005. In only 20 years we will be producing just over one-quarter of the amount of oil which we produce now. It is extremely important for us to eliminate that dependency, not only for cost reasons, but because oil is a finite resource. We must ensure that it will be there for our grandchildren's and children's use.
Three or four years ago this program was agreed to by all Parties. It was unanimously agreed that the program was a good means by which to encourage people to switch from oil to natural gas, wood or another means of heat. The program has run quite well. At its half-way point it has converted half of the targeted homes from their reliance on oil. The program has met its targets and has not been terribly expensive, considering the savings which have been realized.
The program is now saving approximately 42,000 barrels of oil per day, or 15.3 million barrels of oil per year as a result of COSP. Since we consume approximately 1.45 million barrels of oil per day for all energy uses-homes, industry and transportation-it means a net energy saving of about 2.8 per cent. That saving is directly attributable to this program. In fact, the oil which is saved through COSP is enough to heat about
650,000	Canadian homes per year. On average, the homes which have converted have saved about 13.8 barrels of oil per year, which amounts to a saving of $634.80 annually. Therefore, a home owner who converts to oil can expect a return on his investment within three years. However, there are certain circumstances in which that will take longer and it will become more expensive.
Canadians in large numbers were switching from oil to other forms of energy. However, suddenly the new Government made a rapid decision to discontinue the program. What has that done to the spirit of optimism and the expectation of
better things to come for small business people in the business of installing gas lines, furnaces and other forms of heat-producing devices? It has left them in a real quandry. They have been scrambling around since November 8-and they only have until the end of the month-to meet the enormous number of calls for business.
Some of those businesses may have been enticed into hiring more people, but as the program will end on March 31, most of the installers know that hiring more people to meet the rush in an attempt to meet the deadline will not be sustained because it will require them to buy extra service vehicles and tools. Therefore, most of those businesses have not panicked and expanded.
Not only has the termination of this program been disruptive to small business, it has been unfair to home owners. Some home owners prepare their budgets over several years, and many decided to convert toward the end of the program-in the late 1980s-because their furnaces were still working well or they did not immediately have the money to make the switch. Therefore, they decided to delay taking advantage of the program. Those home owners will now have to pay an extra $800 to convert.
In addition, there is a tremendous number of individuals in smaller communities who have not, to this point in time, had gas available to them. They know that the lines have been proposed and are projected, and that in a year or two gas will be in their communities or it will run past their house. But for the moment they do not have the option of switching to gas because they are no gas lines. Those people who were awaiting the gas line to be installed in their communities are now faced with the prospect of not only having to wait longer than most Canadians to switch to the cheaper form of heat, but they are now ineligible for the subsidy of $800 and will have to pay the full cost. That is unfair, Mr. Speaker, particularly when that is a program which was doing so much to shift people away from a depleting resource, namely, light oil. In spite of spending billions an billions of dollars, we have not been able to find replacements for it. Many billions of dollars have been spent in government funds to subsidize and assist with write-off and tax deferrals. We have assisted sometimes to the point of paying in excess of 90 per cent of ail the drilling costs for the search for oil in the Arctic. We have not been terribly successful. We have not come up with answers to the hard fact that we will only be producing 28 per cent of our current output of those kinds of oils in a mere 20 years.
Our only prudent choice would be to find ways of using the limited energy we have-which is becoming more limited as time goes on-in a better way. We should be doing more in the way of insulating our homes. The CHIP program, which will be in effect for a few more months, has assisted in that way.
I will conclude by saying that I believe it is very unfortunate that the Government has chosen to attempt to save a few dollars in the short term by totally closing its eyes to the problems which face us in the production and pricing of
March 21, 1985

energy. This is a very sloppy way of going about producing economy.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke on a motion earlier with respect to this matter and I had hoped at the end that Hon. Members would agree to extend my time so that I could continue to make a few additional remarks. I am happy now to have the opportunity in effect to conclude the thoughts I wanted to put to Hon. Members in an attempt to get the Government to reconsider its decision to cancel these two very important programs.
I would like to agree with the Hon. Member who spoke earlier. He made the point that we are, frankly, wanting to ensure that this Bill takes enough time to get through the House so that the Canadian people can find out what it is that this Government is trying to do to them. What is interesting is that this is a Government which appears to be dedicated to cutting the deficit, and I would like to come back to that theme in a moment. It is a Government as well which is very responsive to angry voters. Two of the "hits" which it has tried to make on existing programs have resulted in very effective reactions which I hope will lead the Government to reconsider. The first is its plan to cut back medical research by something like 20 per cent a year. The medical research community responded by effectively and intelligently demonstrating to the Government and to the Canadian people that the changes which the Government had in mind would lead to researchers moving to the United States because of the effective reduction and eventual elimination of cancer research in our country. This is especially so because the Conservative Government of Ontario is also withdrawing its support for medical research, and the Conservative Government of Alberta, which had been a big sponsor of cancer research, announced that it was going to cut its support for cancer research.
Important scientific breakthroughs have been made in cancer research in our country. There is no doubt that the work which was going on was valid and should be continued. Apart from the research aspect, as these skilled researchers begin to leave our country, we are going to find-
