speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should disallow further Canadian investment in South Africa, outlaw the importation of South African Krugerrand gold coins into Canada and outlaw Canadian bank loans to South Africa.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate that the motion is before the House this afternoon because today the Mayor of Ottawa, Marian Dewar, has declared Thursday, March 21, 1985, International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
It is also important to realize that the General Assembly of the United Nations, in 1979, designated the week beginning March 21 as the week of solidarity with people struggling racism and racial discrimination. That was resolution 3424 of November 15, 1979.
It is important to realize that the Minister responsible for multiculturalism got up in his place in the House today and made a statement proclaiming today International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
It is also significant to note that today is the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre where white police in South Africa opened fire on a crowd of black people who were peacefully demonstrating against the pass law of South Africa. Sixty-nine people were killed, including eight women and ten

March 21, 1985
South Africa
children. There were 186 wounded, including 31 women and 19 children.
It is also significant to note that the CBC news announced just this morning from South Africa that 14 people were killed today by South African white police because those people were demonstrating to commemorate the Sharpeville massacre.
Therefore, it is appropriate that we keep that in mind as a background when discussing this particular motion. The Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) and all Canadians can say many nice things. However, not only do our fellow citizens judge this Parliament and the Government by its actions, the international community also judges Canada by the kind of tough, principled positions that we are prepared to take.
Just last week, for the first time, the United Nations Security Council unanimously passed a resolution condemning South Africa for the deaths of scores of black demonstrators and the arrest of black opposition leaders on treason charges. It was the first time during the Reagan administration that the United States has voted in favour of a resolution in the Security Council condemning the white South African minority Government for its domestic policies. All 15 Security Council members voted in favour of the resolution that strongly condemned the killing of defenceless protesters and the arrest of 16 leaders of the United Democratic Front and other organizations opposed to South Africa's policy of apartheid, which is basically racial discrimination at its worst.
The Security Council also called on South Africa to withdraw the charges of high treason against the leaders of the Front. The very word "apartheid" conveys its meaning-apart. In fact, it is a word that means strict racial segregation. It was imposed in 1958 by the white minority in South Africa.
In 1960 the Bantustans or homelands, as they are now called, were set up. The black people would be relegated to reserves, or homelands and would be allowed to work in the white urban community and be given pass cards. When they were not working they would then return to their homelands. It was in opposition to that in 1960 when we saw the demonstration that resulted in the Sharpeville massacre.
Today there are some 10 of these Bantustans or homelands. They were set up by South Africa, and no other country in the world recognizes them as independent states except South Africa. Five of them are recognized by South Africa as independent. In fact, the black man then, as now, is held as an indentured slave in his own land, to work in domestic corporations for white South African ownership or indentured to work for foreign-owned corporations. Some of those foreign-owned corporations are Canadian, which I will speak about later on. Indeed, the South African black works in the mines that produce the gold which makes the krugerrands which the following banks sell here in Canada: the Bank of Montreal, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Commerce and the Toronto Dominion Bank. They sell this kruggerrand valued at $507 Canadian or $337 U.S.
That we should be a market for coins which are made at the expense of the freedom and dignity of people should not be allowed. We do have a replacement coin which we should be promoting. We have the Maple Feaf gold coin which can be used as a substitute for those who want to invest as entrepreneurs in gold coins. Therefore, we really do not need to allow the sale of krugerrands in this country.
It seems to me that by forbidding the sale of krugerrands in Canada we would send a clear message that we are not prepared to be a silent participator in the oppression of black people in South Africa. In fact, the South African Government has enshrined apartheid in its constitution. It clearly says in its constitution that a black man and a white man are not equal. It says a white man is superior to a black man. Of course, the South African Government uses all sorts of biblical quotations to back up that position. It went on from there to establish all sorts of laws that affect relationships between the races in South Africa and it was used to deny the black man the right to vote.
In our society it seems that we have come a long way. There was a time when we did not allow women to vote. We have gone beyond that, and we in this country recognize that in a democratic free society it has to be one man, one vote.
South Africa refuses to recognize that men are all created equal in the eyes of God. It seems to me just on the one question of allowing the krugerrands to be imported that we are winking, closing and turning a blind eye to our brothers and sisters in South Africa who have been enslaved.
The question of the South African Parliament is rather interesting. To try and give an impression of change, the white South African Government created three changes. It has a white chamber, a chamber for coloureds, and a chamber for Indians or Asians. Again, the black man is denied the right to vote and the right to participate in his own country. When we consider the blacks in South Africa comprise approximately 16 million of the population and the whites 4.5 million, the coloureds 3 million, and the Asians about 1 million, what we have in South Africa is really the oppression of the minority. Every single penny which we repatriate to South Africa as a result of selling krugerrands continues, allows, the white South African Government to entrench itself and to buy the latest and most powerful forms of weaponry, not only to enslave its own black population but to act as a policeman in the southern part of the African continent, to create a climate of disturbance among its black neighbours in southern Africa.
The other area I wanted to turn to was the area of trade. It is significant to note that Canada's second most important trading partner in Africa is South Africa, Algeria is first, South Africa is second. In 1984 Canada imported $201 million worth of goods from South Africa. We exported to South Africa $201 million. They call that balanced trade.
What did we export to South Africa? We exported sulphur, wood pulp, railway rolling stock, machines and motor vehicles. What did we import from South Africa? Iron, steel, sugar,
March 21, 1985

metal ores, concentrates, scrap and manufactured goods. There is nothing among those items that we do not produce in Canada. We do not need to import iron and steel from South Africa. We have iron mines closing in Canada because we do not have steel mill capacity to accept it. We are closing iron ore mines in northwestern Ontario and in Newfoundland, while at the same time we import iron ore from South Africa. Even on a question of domestic economic activity, we are shooting ourselves in the foot.
There are 28 Canadian companies in South Africa. Canada decided that we should have some code of behaviour for Canadian companies operating in South Africa, but it was never legislated. It is just a recommendation that these companies must file on an annual basis a code of conduct. That has been in effect since 1978. Only one of the 28 companies has lived up to filing a code of behaviour, filing an accountability for behaviour. That company is Alcan. Only one, Mr. Speaker, out of 28.
It seems to me that there are very few, comparatively speaking, black South Africans who work in Canadian companies operating in South Africa. In fact, to sever trade with South Africa would not in any way create any economic hardship. Indeed, in my conversations with the African National Congress it was indicated to me that this was the route it would like Canada to go. The African National Congress would approve of Canada severing trade relationship with South Africa. As long as we continue to trade with the racist white South African Government, we are participating in the oppression of the black man in South Africa. We fought a war over that to prove that all men are equal in the eyes of God. We fought over that, yet here we are slipping along with the flow.
Our predecessors in this House have given us a start. They have given us an example. It was two former Prime Ministers who took positions which at that time were quite tough. I have the Hansard reference here for April 27, 1960, in this House when the Hon. Lester B. Pearson, at the time Leader of the Opposition, moved an emergency resolution. This was prior to the Prime Minister, the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, going to the Commonwealth Conference that year. Mr. Pearson moved a resolution to let the Prime Minister know how Members of Parliament felt about South Africa and its participation in the British Commonwealth. In the debate, the Hon. Mr. Chevrier said, talking about apartheid policy:
It is a policy that must cease if normal relations are to be restored in that country of the British commonwealth of nations. Peace, order, and security cannot exist without due respect for the individual.
Peace, order, and security cannot exist, I repeat, without any respect for the individual.
I think it is well that we cast back to what former Leaders and Members in this House said. Mr. Diefenbaker replied:
Mr. Speaker, that is the purpose of this discussion today, to reinforce me as the representative of this nation, having held these views throughout the years, with the conscience, thought and deliberation of the Canadian House of Com-
South Africa
mons in order to air the views which have been expressed on matters which arc of particular moment at this time.
As a matter of fact, it was at that Commonwealth Conference that South Africa was put out of the Commonwealth.
I think we have to carry the torch, the torch which was handed us by former Leaders in this House. The path on which Mr. Pearson and Mr. Diefenbaker put us back in 1960 must be continued. The three particular actions which I am recommending are very important because they will send a message to the rest of the international community, the community of nations, that in fact Canada is prepared to stand up and be counted.
Thank God we have a living example of the kind of courage which cries out to us. It is the courage of Nelson Mandela, the founder of the African National Congress. In 1960, he was arrested and sentenced to life imprisonment on Robin Island for treason. He is still there, 25 years later. The white racist Government of South Africa recently offered him an amnesty provided he revoked his advocacy of violent revolution in South Africa. He refused to do so. His courage in the face of being confined for 25 years, perhaps seeing his wife and family from time to time, cries out to us, white brothers, that we cannot let him down. In fact, we have to bring this thing to a head. We cannot have a minority oppressing a large majority. We cannot have a nation founded on a principle that the white man is superior to the black man. We cannot want for ourselves what we do not want for others.
The heritage of freedom which we enjoy as Canadians, we should want for all peoples of the world. We should be prepared to put our action where our mouth is. I call upon the House to let this motion come to a vote. Let the Government know. It can program in-and it does not have to be done tomorrow-all three specific actions which I have recommended in my motion. I hope it will begin the dawn of a new day, with Canada leading the way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to begin by thanking the Hon. Member. I listened very attentively to his comments, and I commend him on them. Throughout my experience-and it is a rather recent one-he has always been concerned about the rights of ethnics, not only abroad but at home. He has made valuable contributions to the House.
When he speaks about the 25 years since Pearson and Diefenbaker, the 25 years Mr. Mandela has been in prison, it has has also been 25 years when another Government has been in place, another Government which had many opportunities to look at these things. Since September we have continued the policy but promised a review.
Recently I had the pleasure of meeting a delegation of the Quebec task force on immigrant women. It is a group with which I have considerable contact and its social justice committee in Montreal. We discussed many of the same concerns. The response to many of these issues which the group indicated in its bulletin appears positive. Of course the task force will

March 21, 1985
South Africa
be continuing to help me in my work as a part of the Government.
One issue which I brought to a head on February 5 appears under the heading "South Africa" and reads as follows: "Mr. Weiner indicated that South Africa was an area that would be re-examined by the Government". With a green paper about to be deposited and a task force constituted for a review of our foreign policy, we are very hopeful that they will be examining our relationship with South Africa and certainly its over-all effect on the despicable apartheid situation.
It is coincidental, but symbolic, that today's debate is taking place on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre in which 69 people died at the hands of the South African police. March 21 has been fittingly designated by the United Nations as the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. Canadian representatives at United Nations headquarters in New York and Vienna are attending commemoration ceremonies while other Canadians have demonstrated outside the South African Embassy in Ottawa to show their opposition to apartheid. I understand that there has been a tragic incident even today in South Africa in which a number of people have died. Before debating the motion at hand, it would be appropriate for the House to remember those who, over the years, have suffered and in some cases given their lives in the struggle for justice in their own country.
Sharpeville represented a turning point in South Africa's history. Following the unrest, the African National Congress was banned and subsequently turned to violent methods. Some observers believe that South Africa's Government is again facing choices which will have profound consequences for their country's history. It is the responsibility of the Canadian Government to encourage those men, whom Canada's Ambassador to the UN has called a "beleaguered oligarchy", to listen to the voices of moderated among their own population. Further delay in implementing basic reforms will only reduce the chances of peaceful change.
The Canadian Government also faces difficult choices. The concern of the Canadian Government is first and foremost the fate of those we are trying to help, the victims of the apartheid system. It is in light of this criterion, which I am sure Hon. Members on the other side shares, that we must examine seriously the measures proposed by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
Among other elements, this motion calls on the Government of Canada to disallow further Canadian investment in South Africa. Such a proposal reflects the view that investment by multinational enterprises based in Western countries is necessarily supportive of apartheid and does not hasten its dissolution. This hypothesis is open to question and certainly requires careful study. Many opponents of apartheid hold the contrary view. It is important for us to weigh the consequences of our actions. Let us examine the facts.
Multinational corporations have played an important role in South Africa's economic development. According to UN sources, at the end of 1981 there were over $15 billion U.S. of foreign direct investment in South Africa, much of it concentrated in manufacturing and mining and more advanced sectors such as computers and chemicals. In 1982, the U.K. and the U.S.A. were the two largest investors in South Africa with about $2.5 billion. Germany was third with some 799 million Deutschmarks. It is estimated that some 400 U.S. companies have subsidiaries in South Africa and some 600 firms based in the U.K. have operations in South Africa.
According to the latest figures available, which are for 1982, Canadian companies have about $200 million invested, a small percentage of total foreign investment in South Africa. The rate of increase of investments by all foreign companies has slowed in South Africa; the stock of Canadian investment has hardly increased for a number of years. Not only is Canadian investment in South Africa not increasing, some disinvestment is now occurring. There are about 30 Canadian companies with operations in South Africa. Over half of these have minority positions with little or no management control. This suggests that unilateral action by Canada might, in any event, be a hollow gesture without practical effect.
In the Canadian case, the Government's approach to investment in South Africa is based on a number of elements. First and foremost, our opposition to the practice of apartheid has led to an end to the official promotion of commercial and investment relations with the Republic of South Africa.
In the case of trade, restrictive measures date back to 1963. At that time, Canada voluntarily imposed an embargo on sales of arms and military equipment to South Africa. That was extended, in 1970, to include spare parts. In 1977, Canada, then a member of the Security Council, supported the application of a mandatory arms embargo on South Africa.
In addition, in 1977, the Canadian Government decided to end the active promotion of trade and investment in South Africa. The Canadian trade commissioners previously assigned to South Africa were withdrawn and the Consulate-General in Johannesberg was closed. The use of the Export Development Corporation's government account for financing and insuring trade with South Africa was suspended and the facilities which had been available for the insurance of Canadian investments in South Africa were also withdrawn. These measures were further extended when the use of the EDC's corporate account for South Africa was also suspended.
The Canada-South Africa trade agreement, which accorded South African exports preferential tariff access to the Canadian market, has been terminated. Private Canadian companies remain free to trade in peaceful goods with South Africa and to invest there, according to their own judgment.
Second, while it does not encourage trade and investment activity, the Government of Canada is opposed to mandatory economic sanctions against South Africa, including those relating to investment. Such measures would not promote the peaceful and positive change in South Africa which we support; they might, rather, foster violence. They would also seriously harm the disadvantaged black majority in South Africa and the neighbouring states. Those in South Africa are
March 21, 1985

already denied basic political and civil rights: they would surely suffer further economic privation.
The operations of the foreign companies in South Africa have, in many instances, had a positive effect in creating greater wealth among non-whites and in encouraging social change. These companies employ a relatively small percentage of the South African labour force, but when they adopt progressive practices, they set an example to be followed by local investors or establish a benchmark for worker demands throughout the labour force.
Canada has taken some steps to see that this is the case for Canadian companies operating in South Africa. Recognizing that the laws and policies of the South African Government specifically disadvantage non-white workers, Canada's present Code of Conduct makes detailed recommendations with respect to general working conditions, collective bargaining, wages, fringe benefits, training and promotion and race relations. Under the Code of Conduct, companies are invited to make annual public reports in sufficient detail to permit assessment of their progress in realizing the objectives of the code. The code appears to have had some positive effects, but the range of reporting has been limited and could be improved. Consideration is being given to new initiatives designed to make the code a more useful instrument.
In that direction, we may want to have a look at the Proxmire Bill that is now before Congress. Obviously when only one company out of 30 has complied with the voluntary reporting to Parliament, we have to make sure that we look at other options.
There are clear legal limits to the influence that the Canadian Government, and other home Governments, may claim with respect to the activities in South Africa of companies with head offices in their jurisdictions. These companies are subject to the jurisdiction of South Africa with respect to their operations in that country. Canada rejects the extraterritorial assertion of the laws of other countries that inter alia seek to direct the activities of foreign companies operating in Canada in a way that displaces Canadian law and policy. Such practice would be contrary to international law and an infringement on Canadian sovereignty. Canada as a home country, therefore, cannot purport to extend its own law to South African activities of South African companies controlled by Canadian nationals or residents in a way that directly displaces South African law and policy, no matter how objectionable the latter may be. Therefore, we could not enforce any ban on new investments in South Africa based on retained earnings or local borrowing by South African affiliates of Canadian companies. Neither can we, as a country, compel Canadian-controlled companies operating in South Africa to break South African law.
For the same reason, we would be constrained from applying any investment ban to jurisdictions outside Canada where subsidiaries of Canadian companies are operating in order to contain any circumvention by these companies through subsidiaries in countries without such a ban. This could make any ban on Canadian investment in South Africa difficult to
South Africa
enforce and cause concern in friendly countries with a different policy approach about the extraterritorial application of Canadian laws.
On balance, therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Government is not convinced that the banning of new investment to South Africa by Canadian companies is the proper way to register our objection to apartheid. We do, however, feel that Canadian companies that choose to operate in South Africa should do all they can to counter the destructive and dehumanizing effects of apartheid. They can, by this means, contribute to the process of peaceful change in South Africa-to the removal of institutionalized racial discrimination, and the full realization of human rights.
We also have reservations about proposals to ban the sale of kruggerand gold coins in Canada. This issue must be considered in the context of Canadian policy on trade with South Africa and our more general international trade obligations. While the Canadian Government does not as a matter of policy promote trade with South Africa, it does not prevent or restrict trade in peaceful goods and services. The only exceptions are where such activities would contravene sanctions imposed by the Security Council, for example, the mandatory arms embargo adopted in 1977.
In the absence of any international agreement among South Africa's trading partners, such unilateral action might also be considered to be contrary to Canada's obligation under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. This would open the way for legal claims for compensation or retaliating action. As far as can be determined, no Western country has adopted such legislation. For these reasons we do not believe that the institution of a measure restricting peaceful trade would be a constructive or legitimate step to take at this time.
The final measure proposed would outlaw Canadian bank loans to South Africa. I would remind the House that the Canadian Government itself does not lend funds to South Africa. The government account facilities of the Export Development Corporation have been withheld from public sector and private sector buyers in South Africa since December 1977. In 1981, corporate account facilities available to South African buyers were also withdrawn.
A number of Canadian banks have evidently decided on their own-in the context of a dialogue with their shareholders-to suspend loans to the South African Government or coporate borrowers. That is their right, and their risk as private lending institutions in an open economy such as ours. Such action is a prime example of the operation of free and responsible action by independent Canadians exercising their own judgment. That is the kind of open debate which is a credit to the Canadian people and which this Government wishes to encourage. Free public debate and decisions taken by autonomous institutions are obviously preferable to coercive legislation.
I would also note that the rules of international law limit the authority of a state to control or direct conduct in the territory of another state. They make it illegitimate to attempt to

March 21, 1985
South Africa
prohibit lending to South African borrowers in South Africa. The difficulties in enforcing such action are obvious.
I believe it is clear that Canada has already done a good deal to encourage reform in South Africa. In addition to the measures already cited, I would mention the boycott on contacts between nationally representative sporting teams and athletes. This action, taken in conjunction with our Commonwealth partners, has brought home to the ordinary white South African the depth of Canadian and international opposition to apartheid.
One more thing that the Government and Canadians in general can do is to provide support to various groups working with the black community of South Africa. These include some major Canadian churches and non-governmental organizations, the Canadian Labour Congress, and the World University Service of Canada. Self-help projects in rural communities, leadership training and providing scholarships are concrete ways in which we as Canadians can play a constructive part. Our role must be to support those groups inside South Africa which are working to promote peaceful change. We must avoid empty moral gestures or actions which are inconsistent with our international obligations.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would stress that though much has already been done, we mean to continue and to do more. To borrow a phrase from Canada's Ambassador to the United Nations, what is required is unrelenting pressure. That is our policy. This Government has already consulted such prominent South Africans as Bishop Desmond Tutu and Chief Gatsha Buthelezi. We shall continue to look at these questions and to consult with interested parties including Canadians. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) announced to the House on February 15, the Government is reviewing its relations with South Africa. We shall, in that context, take account of the views expressed in this House today.
The Government has promised in the Throne Speech a thorough review of Canada's international relations and that this would involve public consultations. We want to hear Canadians' views on future direction for our foreign policy, including the best approach to the problem of human rights in South Africa. This process will shortly be engaged by a special parliamentary group. Adoption of the current proposals would tend to prejudge the outcome of the review and close off avenues of public debate. That is hardly the right way to proceed.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to stress that the Government's opposition to apartheid is second to none. I would recall that it was a Progressive Conservative Government that sided with the African states in the Commonwealth in preventing South Africa's continued membership in 1961. In 1979 it was a Progressive Conservative Prime Minister who joined other Commonwealth leaders in adopting the Lusaka Declaration on Racism and Racial Discrimination. That was the strongest and clearest affirmation ever adopted by the Commonwealth on this issue.
Our policy is based on the moral issues involved, and on our desire to take effective steps. Apartheid has been described as a stench in the nostrils of the world by one Afrikaner writer. Our sense of the injustices is as keen as that of the Members of the Opposition. I accept no lessons in morality from them in this regard. We all, I trust, seek peaceful change and not destructive violence. Apartheid, however, will not be weakened by empty gestures that make us feel self-satisfied. We want to look at the issues in a realistic manner and will do so as we review the options. Although we do not support the proposed motion, we share the Hon. Member's repugnance of apartheid and his desire to see quicker progress to peaceful change. That, too, is our objective.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members will recall, the resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should disallow further Canadian investment in South Africa, outlaw the importation of South African Krugerrand gold coins into Canada and outlaw Canadian bank loans to South Africa.
I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on a sincere and obviously deeply felt speech. I think he believed each and every word that he said. I wish it could be said that all of us believed all of the things we say in this House all of the time. I believe he was completely sincere in what he said and I salute him for the passion and conviction with which he offered his speech.
Second, Sir, I would make reference to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Weiner). I would remind the House that it is well known that as Mayor of Dollard, the Hon. Member was particularly active in a Montreal area committee which was trying to ensure that visible minorities have a better chance to be hired by the Montreal and District Police Force. It is well known that one of the reasons he was elected to the House against a majority of something in the order of 35,000 was that he was recognized as being a person who stands for the rights of all Canadians, whatever their colour, race, background or creed, to have equal rights with every other Canadian. He is a person who, like the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, believes in action more than in talk in this sphere as in many others.
One of the best reasons apartheid is despicable is that it equates inferiority with an irremovable natural quality, pigmentation, and persists in the goal of white supremacy even in circumstances which make the attainment of that goal impossible without evil means such as torture. As well, apartheid is a stench in the nostrils of humanity, as mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary. That is why it is despicable. Each and every Member of the House, I would think, despises it as much as the Hon. Member fo Nickel Belt, the Hon. Member for Dollard, and I.
I recently spent time in three African countries, Gabon, Zaire and Ethiopia, and I have spent a great deal of time lately reading about Africa in an attempt to know it better than I did before. South Africa is anathema to southern Africa for the very reasons that have been mentioned by both previ-
March 21, 1985

ous speakers. Any self-respecting person of any colour despises a system which gives preference to one race and discriminates against another race.
As the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt knows, one of the problems the West has with South Africa is that by being perceived to be in favour of an abhorrent regime in South Africa, we are seen as being on the wrong side of an issue vitally important to about 600 million people who live in the continent of Africa. That is a very major obstacle, quite aside from its implications in terms of the people who are jailed like Joseph Mandela or many other South Africans who have suffered as well.
I do not think it was mentioned that this Party has a long and honourable tradition on this issue. I would remind the Hon. Member that it was the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker who saw to it that South Africa was driven out of the Commonwealth in 1961. With very few exceptions, we have made it clear from the beginning where we stand on this issue and it is very close to the position of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt.
When Archbishop Trevor Huddleston was here a few months ago, and later on his godson, Bishop Tutu, it was an honour and a privilege for me to spend several hours with both of them and to learn more clearly of their insights into this problem. Bishop Tutu tells us that South Africans, when they finally overcome this cancer, will look to see who sided with them and who sided against them and they will know who their friends are and who their friends are not. That sort of a remark touches the hearts of all of us.
1 would remind the Hon. Member that even Bishop Tutu has said that he will give the Government 18 months in which to do something. The Hon. Member may say that that is because he will go to jail if he says otherwise, but Bishop Tutu has said that if nothing is done in 18 months, he will call for disinvestment from South Africa. If he is prepared to give South Africa a little more time, although the Hon. Member may ask how much time is enough, perhaps that is something that Canadians should consider as well.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: They had 25 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I know. You're absolutely right.
The Hon. Member is speaking about outlawing bank loans to South Africa. I am told that Canadian Schedule A banks have $180 billion in outstanding loans in all countries around the world. While I do not have a specific figure for South Africa, it is less than one-tenth of 1 per cent of that total amount. It is a drop in the bucket.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Still too much.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that it is still too much. Can we outlaw a loan to, for example, XYZ company, a company in South Africa that employs black people? Would that help the cause of black men, women and children in South Africa? How does that help the people at the bottom of the economic heap? Obtaining a loan from Canada might make
South Africa
the difference between the business continuing or not. How does it help to tell the company it can no longer obtain loans from Canada?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Are you kidding me? The United States forbade American banks to lend money to Cuba.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The Hon. Member already had a chance to speak. I do not mind the occasional heckling, but 1 would ask him not to do it every four seconds. If he does, I will be doing nothing but answering his questions.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: You're running out my time anyway so what does it matter?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: If we cut off bank loans, would that do anything for the people whom we are trying to help, which is the people at the bottom?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The Hon. Member said "yes". I guess this Government says no.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: We know whose friend you are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I would remind the Hon. Member that Ambassador Stephen Lewis and I spent a week together in law school, back when he was smart enough to get out of law school. On November 20, Ambassador Lewis, said in the United Nations, on behalf of the Government, that the Canadian Government rejects the concept that total isolation of South Africa would somehow promote fundamental reform in that country. It would not happen. Racist mentalities feeds on isolation. Isolation breeds the kind of defiance which further fans the flames of oppression and hatred. If the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt accepts that reasoning-and I hope he does as I believe that most Members of the House accept that reasoning-then how can we help the cause by cutting off all connections with South Africa?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The Hon. Member said "right", but do we do the same thing with Cuba? What about Nicaragua?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The Americans did.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
That is the point. The Americans did. But, I always thought that it was the policy of all Members of the House that wherever possible we wanted to keep our contacts with Governments with which we profoundly disagree.
Do we say to the Government of Haiti-where, as he knows, human rights are probably breached more than anywhere else-that we will no longer have anything to do with it?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Next on the list.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
By that, we will help the Haitians-

March 21, 1985
South Africa

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I think we would send a message to the Government of Haiti and it would be an effective message.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: That is not realistic.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
One Member said that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt is unrealistic. I think it is the Canadian tradition, which is shared by all Parties, that we try wherever possible to keep our contacts and to keep the flow of communications open with as many countries as we can. I repeat, racist mentalities feed on isolation. Isolation breeds the kind of defiance which further fans the flames of oppression and hatred.
The second part of the resolution asks us to outlaw the importation of South African krugerrand gold coins to Canada. My understanding-and perhaps the Hon. Member can correct me-is that the gold coins are 100 p. cent gold. If that is the case, there is nothing easier on the face of the earth than to melt the coins down and simply bring in the gold in its natural metal form. I do not know how the second part of his resolution will-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Ban the importation of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: We cannot ban the importation of gold.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: From South Africa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: If the Hon. Member believes that gold coming from South Africa should be banned-and I believe that South Africa produces something like 20 per cent of the world's gold supply-then we can simply say that no Canadian will buy gold if it had its origin in South Africa.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: We have gold mines in Ontario.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The third question is to disallow further Canadian investment in South Africa. I have indicated as clearly as I can that with investment in South Africa, as the Parliamentary Secretary indicated, if the companies are required to provide equal access to facilities for white and black people, then that is helping the people about whom we are concerned.
I do not want to be accused of talking this motion out. I agree with what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs said and I agree with large chunks of what the the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt said.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid it is I who will be forced to talk this motion out this afternoon. I do not think that it is something that the Government of Canada can accept, for the reasons which were expressed by the Parliamentary Secretary.
In particular, on this side of the House, we have to give deep consideration to the various ramifications that a policy such as that proposed by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) would have. When I read his motion, it occurred to me that it was some kind of a knee-jerk reaction to something
which he does not like any more than does the vast majority of Canadians. But I fail to see how in doing this we would have any influence whatsoever on the policies of a foreign and sovereign Government.
It would seem that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has perceived the problem and wants to turn his back on it. If he does not see it any more, and if there are no relations between Canada and South Africa, then he thinks it will go away. But I do not think that will happen.
If Canada and other Western countries decided to turn their backs completely on South Africa, things would continue very much the same as they are now. There would not be a general improvement in the situation, which has happened to some extent. By all accounts, there is a general improvement which has happened from time to time. Sure, there is a long way to
go-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Tell us about the improvements.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The Hon. Member asked me to tell him about the improvements. I would ask him to contrast the fate of some of the people for which he is so concerned in South Africa to those in other countries. We know what is going on in Ethiopia and Uganda. I believe that a lot of people in Ethiopia would much prefer to live in South Africa, despite the fact that political rights would not be available to them. At least they could eat, get a fairly good job and have a roof over their heads.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Are you serious?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Of course I am serious. I would suggest that the Hon. Member, too, should be serious. Perhaps he is not concerned with the plight of people in Ethiopia. Perhaps he is not concerned with what happened in Uganda. We do not want a revolution, bloodshed and that type of thing. We do not want to force that on people. We want an improvement in the situation.
I would like to take a look at some of the proposals which have been made. We do not want any more Canadian investment in South Africa. We do not want people to go there and develop factories or anything of that nature. But if we really looked at what has been happening, we would see that it is in the foreign-owned factories and the foreign-owned industrial establishments that most of the improvements have been made.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Like the Bata Shoe Company?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
For example, we could look at some of the oil refinery companies in South Africa. A number of those operations have conducted their affairs in a way which shows that there can be racial harmony in South Africa. If one plant can do that, then the people in the next plant will not be frightened and will adopt the same way of operating. Gradually, over a period of time, more plants will adopt that kind of operation.
March 21, 1985

Some of the industrialists in South Africa have been at the forefront of the movement against apartheid. Particularly in the mining industry, people such as Harry Oppenheimer were against it. I know the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt would not approve of a capitalist-industrialist who invests money and creates jobs to allow things to flourish and provide employment for all people of all colours and all races.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CESSATION OF MONETARY TRANSACTIONS WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Exploiting the black man.

That is the very area from which the maximum opposition to apartheid within South Africa has come. It has come from the industrial sector rather than the agricultural sector.
The Hon. Member wants to outlaw the importation of South African gold coins to Canada. The previous speaker gave objections to that proposal and explained how it would be ineffective. subtopic: AGRICULTURE-MARITIME FARMERS COUNCIL S REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY FUNDING. (B) TIMING OF DECISION
AGRICULTURE-MARITIME FARMERS COUNCIL S REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY FUNDING. (B) TIMING OF DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make my comments as a result of a question I posed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on March 14 regarding the Maritime Farmers Council. I wish to point out to the House that I have raised this matter on previous occasions, as has my colleague, the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson).
I raised the matter on February 14 expressing concern that the Maritime Farmers Council is in need of emergency funding which has not been forthcoming by the Government. I also posed a question to the Minister responsible for the Treasury Board on March 8, 1985, and again an answer was not forthcoming. Consequently, I rise with respect to my most recent question on March 14 when I asked the Minister of Agriculture for emergency funding for the Maritime Farmers Council.
By way of background, Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members of both the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party met here in Ottawa in February with representatives of the Maritime
Adjournment Debate
Farmers Council which made its presentation regarding the situation in which it presently finds itself. I believe there was a consensus reached by Hon. Members of both the Liberal and the Conservative Parties who were in attendance that we would all attempt to work for the betterment of the maritime farmers. To date there have been no positive answers forthcoming to those questions. I alluded to the fact that the indefinite delay by the Minister of Agriculture is the equivalent of a "no" in terms of an answer.
For the benefit of Hon. Members of the House who are here, what is the crisis? The crisis is that at least half of our maritime pork industry will disappear before the end of 1986 unless preventive measures are taken immediately. In Nova Scotia, for instance, at least 25 per cent of our pork producers are already technically bankrupt. The total of their loans and mortgages is greater than the current market value of their assets. A similar situation prevails in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
A 50 per cent reduction in our pork production will seriously threaten the continued viability of one or more of our three major meat packing plants as well as the proposed new plant on Prince Edward Island. Allowing the situation to continue will threaten an industry which currently provides 6500 on-farm jobs with an annual farm gate value of $375 million. If one applies a multiplier effect of three, our maritime livestock industry generates more than $1 billion in annual economic activity within the region. A large portion of this activity is under imminent danger of extinction.
What is the cause of this crisis, Mr. Speaker? I believe there are two causes. In the case of pork, part of the cause is the extended current low market price for pork throughout the North American market. Second, there is a great disparity in feed costs between the Maritimes and the rest of Canada, particularly Ontario. I wish to give a few examples.
On February 1, 1985, according to information provided by the Livestock Feed Board of Canada, the average cost of hog grower ration in Ontario was $207 per tonne, compared with $254 in the Maritimes. That is a difference of $47 per tonne. In the case of dairy cattle, the spread in the cost of dairy ration between the Maritimes and Ontario as of February 1, 1985, was $58 per tonne. This translates to an average increase of 2.9 cents per litre in the production cost of milk in the Maritimes as compared with Ontario. For milk sold for manufacturing purposes, producers in both areas receive essentially the same price. In the fresh fluid market higher prices simply discourage consumption.
What about the case of broilers? The price spread there is the cost of feed. The difference between the Maritimes and Ontario is $53 per tonne, causing a production cost difference of six cents per kilogram.
What about eggs? The price disparity in the cost of laying mash between the Maritimes and Ontario is now $31 per tonne. This means an increased cost of production equivalent to six cents per dozen in the Maritimes over Ontario. The

March 21, 1985
Adjournment Debate
market price for eggs in the Maritimes is less than five cents higher than the Ontario price.
The way to resolve this dilemma, and I believe this is the long-term solution, is to grow all of our feed grains and concentrates. This process has already started. Between 1976 and 1984 our grain acreage has increased from 280,562 to 295,500. Our acreage of protein crops has increased over the same period from practically nothing to approximately 5,000. If we can return to our 1941 acreage of more than 500,000, producing above average yields of barley, wheat, grain corn and soya beans, we could be almost self-sufficient.
However, in order to ensure the survival of our livestock and poultry industries until we do reach self-sufficiency we require an immediate emergency program consisting of the following two items. We have to restore feed grain assistance to the 1975-76 level of funding to cover over 60 per cent of the cost of transportation of feed grains and protein concentrates imported into the Maritimes from central and western Canada. Secondly, we have to extend the same level of assistance to the feed grains and proteins grown within the Maritime region in order to stimulate local production.
In conclusion, Canadians in the Atlantic provinces are not resentful of the huge payouts made to western farmers, whether under the western grain stabilization legislation or others. What we are resentful of is that it is taking so long for the Minister of Agriculture to give an affirmative answer to the request agreed to by both the Conservative and Liberal Parties when we met with the Maritime Farmers' Council. They need an additional $13.5 million of emergency funding. I believe it is high time the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary give an affirmative response to this request in the best interests of the Maritime farmers. I plead for the assistance to be forthcoming now. It this continues to drag on it will amount to saying no to a request which is in the best interests of our region. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to give an affirmative reply forthwith.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-MARITIME FARMERS COUNCIL S REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY FUNDING. (B) TIMING OF DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always amazed to see the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) so eager to applaud his colleague from Cape Breton-Richmond East (Mr. Dingwall). He seemed less inclined to do so when the previous Government adopted all the measures that plunged this country into an accumulated deficit of $200 billion, and an annual deficit of $35 billion we are trying very hard to reduce. He was not applauding last year. Spending was easy at the time. Spending is always easy. Acting responsibly before the Canadian people is something else.
The federal Government did not turn down the request made by the Maritime Farmers' Council. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) had a meeting with the Ministers of Agriculture from the Maritimes, and he met with them again this week to discuss various problems confronting the agricultural industry, both in the Maritimes and in Western Canada.
The Minister has designated an official departmental representative who will work together with the Maritime Provinces and the Maritime Farmers' Council on formulating proposals for dealing with their problems.
When we talk about consensus and discussion and reaching a settlement... of course, our Opposition friends do not even know the meaning of the word "consensus". The word was forgotten for 20 years. Provinces, farmers, everyone was forgotten. This Government has now reopened discussions with the farmers and the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot settle everything in a matter of weeks, because of our tremendous financial problems, as I mentioned before.
The Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has started a review of the Government's feed grains policy. All organizations concerned have been contacted, and each one has been asked to state its position on our policy. The Minister has also offered to meet with as many organizations as possible before undertaking any policy review. That is how this Government operates, not by governing and making decisions and checking afterwards whether people agree. We have said goodbye and good riddance to that approach. This Government has started consulting with people and working together with Canadians. Of course it takes people by surprise. They are not used to it. There are people alive today who never have seen the like of it since their childhood. It just did not exist before. But it is going to exist. People are starting to realize that in Canada we can discuss problems and talk things over. And despite our tremendous problems and our limited financial resources, we have already taken a number of measures that will benefit farm producers in the Maritimes and across Canada.
Federal Government expenditures on agriculture in the Maritimes were estimated at $90 million in 1982 and 1983, out of a total of $1.9 billion. Expenditures for the Maritimes alone, Mr. Speaker, represented 14 per cent of the Government's gross revenue, while it was 9 per cent for Quebec and 4 per cent for Ontario. When the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Richmond East (Mr. Dingwall) says that we are not doing anything for the Maritimes, that is a lot of nonsense. It is just not true. We are going to work for the Maritimes just as we are going to work for the entire country, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS ABOUT CLOSURE OF AIR SAFETY OFFICE IN MONTREAL. (B) EFFECTS OF BUDGETARY CUTS ON MONTREAL
AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS ABOUT CLOSURE OF AIR SAFETY OFFICE IN MONTREAL. (B) EFFECTS OF BUDGETARY CUTS ON MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise at this time to debate the closure of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board office, because our colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Blais), who just answered a question from my colleague from the Maritimes, tried to hide behind the smokescreen of consultation to reply to my colleague and
March 21, 1985

explain the Government's inaction. The issue I want to raise has to do, first, with a decision made by the Conservative Government without any consultation, second, with a broken election promise.
As it happens, the Member for Bellechasse just said that there will be consultation in future. Well, I am saying that when the Conservative Government closed the Canadian Aviation Safety Board office in Montreal, it did not keep its promise to consult the parties involved. For the record, here is the telegram sent to the Minister of State (Transport) (Mr. Bouchard) on November 6, 1984:
We have just learned that you have decided to move the Montreal head office of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.
We would like to know the reasons for such a decision which you made without any consultation with the interested people in the region.
Your Government promised that it would promote dialogue and consultation concerning any decision likely to affect our region.
We are wondering why the consultation process has not been respected as promised.
The Hon. Member for Bellechasse (Mr. Blais) was referring only a few seconds ago to the consultation process so dear to the Tory Government. Well, in this case there has been no consultation.
And that letter is signed by the Mayor of Montreal, Mr. Jean Drapeau, the Chairman of the Montreal Urban Community, Mr. Pierre DesMarais II, the President of the Montreal Commerce Bureau, Mr. Stephen Cheasley, the President of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Philip O'Brien, and the Minister in the Quebec Provincial Government, Mr. Guy Tardif, Minister of Housing and Consumer Protection and Senior Minister from the Greater Montreal area that is affected by this unilateral action taken by the Tory Government, with a loss of some 110 jobs in Metro-Montreal.
In my view, that decision was made for the sole purpose of gratifying a few employees, a few civil servants, a few employees in the Department of Transport, the Transport Commission and the Pilots Association. It is a bad decision and it should never have been made by this Government. It hurts Montreal, and not only does it fly in the face of that consultation commitment but also it goes against the promise made by the Tory Leader when he was in Place Ville-Marie in August telling Montrealers that he would give back to Montreal its status as a metropolis. Well, since he made that commitment to give back to Montreal its status as a metropolis, decision after decision after decision has been made by those ministers to discourage and jeopardize employment in Metro-Montreal.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in the present context, some 10,000 jobs in the transport and aeronautic areas are in jeopardy as a result of those ruthless decisions taken by the Progressive Conservative government, those budget cuts imposed on departments and Crown corporations with headquarters in Montreal.
Adjournment Debate
I urge the member from Quebec who will answer my question to have enough courage to uphold the interests of Quebec and to say to the Progressive Conservative ministers who, one after the other, take administrative decisions having adverse effects on employment in Montreal that this has been going on long enough and that things must change. If it goes on like this, jobs will be lost at Via Rail, at the CN, at Air Canada, at Canadair, at Teleglobe and in the port of Montreal as a result of budgetary reductions made by the Conservative government. This cannot go on. May I remind the House that the headquarters of the International Civil Aviation Organization are in Montreal and that the ICAO has acquired a worldwide reputation in the aeronautic as well as in the aerospace areas during the past years. This fact greatly contributes to make Montreal an important city and that is why the previous Liberal government chose that city for the Canadian Air Safety Office. Now I am asking the government to reconsider its decision and to move back to Montreal that important Air Safety Office to make it independent of the Department of Transport and federal officials. It is not only by accident that we have decided to set up that office far from the Canadian capital because there must be a so-called arm's length relation between such an organization and the Department of Transport. I think that the government has underestimated the importance of protecting the independence of that office from the Department of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission. Consequently, I hope that the government will reconsider its decision and will try to create jobs rather than unemployment as it is now doing in Montreal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS ABOUT CLOSURE OF AIR SAFETY OFFICE IN MONTREAL. (B) EFFECTS OF BUDGETARY CUTS ON MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard once again the Official Opposition trying to alarm Canadian people by saying that 10,000 jobs are being threatened. In fact, it is the 20 million, or rather 25 million Canadians who were being threatened until September 4 by disastrous economic policies which resulted in an incredible deficit, but the Members opposite do not like us to talk about it. They always say that we are trying to rewrite history, when we mention it.
Mr. Speaker, to paraphrase my colleague from Frontenac, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), I replied to the first question of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) by rising. As for courage, it indeed takes some courage to take over the economic situation and the country in the state where you left it, but we have that courage and we shall have it for a long time. You can be sure of that.
First, let us put certain things in context, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board was created following the recommendations of the Dubin Report on air safety. This is not an economic, industrial or commercial organization, but a board with near judiciary powers. As concerns the investigation of accidents and incidents involving civil airplanes in Canada, the staff of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board were

March 21, 1985
Adjournment Debate
formerly part of Transport Canada. By its nature, the Board must include a technical section supported by its own laboratory, as well as ground testing and checking facilities.
I am convinced that the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) is aware of this. He was a member of the Government long enough to know it. It is impossible that he should not be aware of it. The laboratory and facilities are already located in Ottawa. There was never any question about moving them to Montreal. They are already located in Ottawa. We see no operational advantage in moving these facilities to Montreal.
In relation to the International Civil Aviation Organization, I can say that the Board already has computer access to its data bank, and in any case, there would be very few contacts between the two agencies. As for establishing the independence and the credibility of the Board, we believe that its performance and not its location will be the determining factor. What is important is not the location, but the effectiveness of the Board. This is obvious. The majority of those with whom the Board has dealings are located in the Ottawa-Hull region. These are the Air Transport Association, the Air Traffic Controllers' Association, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Owners' and Pilots' Association, the Aerospace Industries Association of Canada, the Canadian Transport Commission, Transport Canada and the Department of National Defence. All these agencies are located in the Ottawa-Hull region. Why scare people by saying that another monster has taken away a business from Montreal? A figure of 10,000 jobs was mentioned. The Members opposite are making mountains out of molehills.
Yesterday, the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) spoke about having G.I. Joes sitting in cockpits 24 hours a day on Baffin Island. The Members opposite always try to make mountains out of molehills. That is what is wrong. The new Government must go slowly and take things in stride instead of scaring people over nothing, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: TERRORISM-PROTECTION OF TURKISH EMBASSY. (B) SECURITY ARRANGEMENTS
TERRORISM-PROTECTION OF TURKISH EMBASSY. (B) SECURITY ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in the late show because yesterday Hon. Members of the House and I were given totally unacceptable answers to questions relating to the Turkish Embassy incident, the tragedy which occurred last week when a Canadian security guard was killed. The Government claimed through two of its Ministers that security had been increased about a month before, either in late February or early March, in response to some requests by the Turkish Government, and that the Turkish Government was satisfied with the increase in security. For example, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Neilsen) said, as reported at page 2969 of Hansard, that increased security was provided as recently as last month. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) gave similar assurances to the House.
It is important whether or not they were increased because the Government is obliged under treaty to provide adequate protection to the Turkish Embassy, and because someone died; the family of the victim is entitled to know that the Government did what it could to try to protect that embassy. The Government has claimed that it did. It is important that those claims be validated.
What do we have on the other side? The claims that there was increased security are contradicted by Inspector Paradis of the RCMP, the inspector in charge of VIP security in the whole Ottawa region. The claims of these two Ministers are contradicted by Pinkerton's, and then are contradicted by the Turkish Government which continued to agitate and even sought a meeting with the Minister, but were fobbed off, I believe, on to his Parliamentary Secretary for a discussion. We have these contradictions of the two assertions by the Ministers.
I put it to the Ministers, that their credibility requires that they give some details of the increase in security, what was actually done. We are prepared to believe what was done, but tell us what was done. What did the Minister say? He could not tell me because, first, to do so would compromise national security. If I were asking what the current security arrangements are and the Minister gave that information that would compromise national security. Any interested potential terrorist would know what he is confronted with, but I am not asking about current security arrangements. I am asking about past security arrangements.
I would like to know how giving the details of past security arrangements, not what increases were provided by this Government, would do anything but enhance national security and bring a great deal of relief to the family of the victims, who would then know that something had been done to try to improve the security at the Turkish Embassy. It would also provide a basis for defending our honour as a country with Turkey, the country whose embassy was violated by the terrorist act of last week.
The Minister said that when there appears to be a discrepancy involving the word of an Hon. Member, the word of the Hon. Member is accepted. In other words, the RCMP are liars, the Pinkerton's people are liars and the Turkish Government are liars because they differ with me, says the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and his word has to be accepted.
I suppose if the Secretary of State for External Affairs came into the House and said that today was Sunday, we would have to take his word for that. In these circumstances, the Minister and the Government have no alternative and no reason for not standing up and telling us what increase in security they claim to have provided at the Turkish Embassy.
I want to refer them to a statement the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) made to Canadian Press on March 13, that after many years of almost uninterrupted power they, meaning the Liberals, left us a pretty sorry legacy in security matters. I do not agree with that. However, if that is what the Govern-
March 21, 1985

ment thought in September when they took over, why did they not do something about it? If they thought they had been left a sorry legacy in security matters, why did they sit on an RCMP report requesting additional money for increased security, and not take it to Cabinet?
As recently as last week the Solicitor General said that that report, which I commissioned, had not been taken to Cabinet yet for approval. It flies in the face of reason that this Government can be taking security seriously, as it says it is.
The Parliamentary Secretary is here today. He knows the story. He had a meeting with the Turkish ambassador. I wonder if he might tell us whether he had that meeting because the Minister was too busy or was unwilling to see the Turkish ambassador and what in effect this Government did to to increase the security at the Turkish Embassy, as the Deputy Prime Minister said they did in late February or early March.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TERRORISM-PROTECTION OF TURKISH EMBASSY. (B) SECURITY ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by commenting specifically on the statement of the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) on my meeting with the ambassador. I take my duties and role as Parliamentary Secretary very seriously. The jobs and initiatives that I have been assigned and taken on I do with the utmost of diligence, not because they are flogged on me or because the Minister happens to be busy.
I happen to play a role of liaison to the diplomatic community. This means that each and every ambassador and high commissioner when coming to this country is afforded the opportunity of being able to meet with me to begin a line of communication, which we will continue, and the opportunity of discussing our bilateral relations and our areas of concern. We do this through the forum of meetings in my office, or we may have lunches that are planned with groups of ambassadors or high commissioners, or through any such opportunities I may have to speak to groups.
The meeting held on February 27 between Ambassador Kerdja and myself was very much in keeping with that policy. I had already met a dozen ambassadors of foreign missions. I made it very clear to the Minister, because I gave him a copy of the minutes of that meeting, that there was no discussion of the security or the lack of security at that embassy. We discussed our bilateral relations. We discussed the relationship
Adjournment Debate
between the two countries as it relates to trade potential, the need for increasing trade and our relationship with Turkey as a NATO ally.
I would like to confirm for my hon. friend that when I am involved in these meetings I take them very seriously, as I did my meeting today with the U.N. ambassador from the central African republic. I will continue to play that role as long as the Government and the Secretary of State provide me with that opportunity. That is one of many roles which I have been afforded.
To return to the Hon. Member's question, the investigation ordered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on March 15 about possible approaches to the Government since February 13 by officials of the Turkish Embassy regarding the security of their mission was rapidly carried out and the Secretary of State for External Affairs reported its findings to the House on March 20. As the Minister told the House in his statement on Tuesday, there were two further contacts between Turkish and Canadian officials after mid-February. Although Ministers were not involved with these contracts, the RCMP were. In both cases, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police acted immediately to increase their vigilance, although no new information had been added by the Turkish Embassy to that made available in mid-February.
Although naturally we understand the Hon. Member's concern about this tragic situation, I do not see the relevance of the Hon. Member's reiterated questioning on this aspect. As for getting into the details of security arrangements, past, present and future, I must ask Hon. Members to understand that neither this House nor any public forum is an appropriate place for such discussions. The effectiveness of security measures is not served by allowing to become known information as to what is involved in routine or standard security arrangements, or as to what modifications are made to them when there is cause for increased vigilance. If we were to make that information available, we would run the risk of jeopardizing the safety of those we seek to protect.
